# How to use this guide

Advanced Instrumentation Techniques is **one of the semester-8 electives** of the PCI B.Pharm course. It has no practical; the whole subject is the 75-mark theory paper. It builds directly on Instrumental Methods of Analysis (BP701T, semester 7): you are expected to remember UV, IR, fluorimetry, flame photometry, HPLC and GC from that subject, because Unit 3 asks how those instruments are calibrated and Unit 5 couples HPLC and GC to a mass spectrometer. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, draw each block diagram from memory, redo the worked calculations, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 1 joins NMR and mass spectrometry and Unit 2 joins thermal methods with X-ray diffraction, as the syllabus does; both are long, so their notes are longer. Unit 4 joins radioimmunoassay with extraction techniques.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a diagram and applications.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 NMR and MS | Principle of NMR, chemical shift and the factors affecting it, spin–spin coupling and coupling constant, relaxation, FT-NMR instrumentation, ¹³C NMR (decoupling, DEPT); MS principle, ionisation (EI, CI, FAB, MALDI), fragmentation, quadrupole and TOF analysers |
| 2 Thermal and XRD | TGA, DTA and DSC (principle, instrumentation, factors, applications), DTA vs DSC; origin of X-rays, crystal systems and Miller indices, Bragg's law, rotating crystal, single crystal and powder methods, polymorphism |
| 3 Calibration and validation | Definitions, ICH Q2 validation parameters, qualification (DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ), calibration of balance, UV-visible, IR, fluorimeter, flame photometer, HPLC and GC |
| 4 RIA and extraction | Principle, components, methods and limitations of RIA; LLE and SPE (principle, steps, comparison) |
| 5 Hyphenated techniques | GC-MS/MS and LC-MS/MS instrumentation and interfaces, ESI and APCI, MS/MS scan modes and MRM, HPTLC-MS |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Use one plan for every technique question: **principle → block diagram → each part explained → factors or limitations → applications in pharmacy**. Examiners give separate marks to the diagram.
2. Learn the key equations with every symbol: ν = γB0/2π, δ = Δν/ν(spectrometer) × 10⁶, nλ = 2d sinθ, d = a/√(h² + k² + l²), t = L√(m/2zeV), LOD = 3.3σ/S, LOQ = 10σ/S, K = Corg/Caq.
3. Practise the worked calculations: chemical shift from Hz, J from line positions, m/z of fragments and isotope ratios, % mass loss in TGA, d-spacing from 2θ, recovery and RSD, minimum weight of a balance, fraction extracted after n extractions. Show the formula, substitution and unit.
4. Comparisons are favourite short questions: ¹H vs ¹³C NMR, EI vs CI, quadrupole vs TOF, DTA vs DSC, TGA vs DSC, powder vs single crystal, calibration vs validation, RIA vs IRMA, LLE vs SPE, ESI vs APCI, GC-MS vs LC-MS. Answer them as tables.
5. For Unit 3, write the standard material for each instrument (holmium, potassium dichromate, KCl, toluene in hexane, polystyrene, quinine sulfate, NaCl/KCl standards, caffeine) and what each one checks.
6. Learn the standard numbers: TMS δ 0, ¹H range 0–12 ppm and ¹³C 0–220 ppm, EI at 70 eV, Cl 3 : 1 and Br 1 : 1, tropylium m/z 91, Cu Kα about 1.54 Å, indium mp 156.6 °C, ¹²⁵I half-life about 60 days, assay range 80–120%.
7. End with pharmacy applications (structure, impurity, polymorph, bioanalysis, quality control); the examiner looks for that link.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these with full diagrams: **NMR principle with chemical shift, factors and spin–spin coupling**, **mass spectrometer with EI/CI and quadrupole/TOF**, **DSC (with TGA and DTA)**, **Bragg's law with powder and single crystal methods**, **ICH validation parameters**, **calibration of UV-visible spectrophotometer and HPLC**, **RIA principle**, **SPE steps** and **LC-MS/MS with ESI/APCI**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

**Comparisons in one line each**

- **¹H vs ¹³C NMR:** 99.98% vs 1.1% abundance; 0–12 vs 0–220 ppm; integration reliable vs not; splitting shown vs decoupled singlets.
- **EI vs CI:** high energy, many fragments, M⁺• may be absent vs proton transfer from reagent gas, [M + H]⁺, few fragments.
- **Quadrupole vs TOF:** DC + RF mass filter, unit resolution vs flight time, unlimited range, pairs with MALDI.
- **TGA vs DSC:** mass change vs heat flow; dehydration and decomposition vs melting, Tg, polymorphs, purity.
- **DTA vs DSC:** ΔT, qualitative vs heat flow, quantitative enthalpy.
- **Powder vs single crystal XRD:** fingerprint of crystal form vs complete 3D structure.
- **Calibration vs validation:** instrument accuracy vs fitness of a method or process.
- **RIA vs IRMA:** labelled antigen, limited antibody, competitive, signal falls vs labelled antibody in excess, non-competitive, signal rises.
- **LLE vs SPE:** two liquids, large solvent use, emulsions vs solid sorbent, little solvent, easy automation.
- **GC-MS vs LC-MS:** volatile compounds, EI, libraries vs polar non-volatile compounds, ESI/APCI, bioanalysis.

**Fifteen-minute self-test**

1. A signal is 1260 Hz from TMS on a 300 MHz instrument. What is δ? (4.20 ppm)
2. Why does an alkyne proton appear upfield of an alkene proton? (Anisotropy: the π cylinder shields along the axis.)
3. Give the splitting of the CH2 in ethyl acetate. (Quartet; 3 neighbours.)
4. A compound shows m/z 156 and 158 in 1 : 1 ratio. What does it contain? (One bromine.)
5. Calculate the % mass loss when CuSO4·5H2O loses all its water. (90.1/249.7 × 100 ≈ 36.1%.)
6. Cu Kα (1.5406 Å) gives a peak at 2θ = 20°. What is d? (4.44 Å)
7. Name the standard used to check UV absorbance accuracy. (Potassium dichromate.)
8. Which RIA separation uses an anti-IgG? (Double antibody method.)
9. Which ESI ion would a 15,000 Da protein carrying 10 protons give? (m/z about 1501.)
10. Name the two scans of a triple quadrupole used for quantitation. (SRM/MRM: Q1 and Q3 both fixed.)

questions.answer:
1. Principle: nuclei with spin (I ≠ 0, e.g. ¹H, ¹³C with I = 1/2) behave as tiny magnets. In a field B0 they take 2I + 1 orientations (α with the field, β against it); the energy gap ΔE = hγB0/2π.
2. Nuclei precess at the Larmor frequency ν = γB0/2π. Radio waves of exactly this frequency flip α to β: resonance. A 7.05 T magnet gives about 300 MHz for ¹H.
3. Populations are nearly equal (Boltzmann), so the signal comes from a tiny excess; relaxation (T1, T2) restores it.
4. Shielding: circulating electrons create a field opposing B0; B(eff) = B0(1 − σ). Shielded protons resonate upfield (right), deshielded downfield (left).
5. Chemical shift: δ (ppm) = [ν(sample) − ν(TMS)]/ν(spectrometer) × 10⁶; independent of field strength. Example: 2190 Hz at 300 MHz → 7.30 ppm.
6. TMS as reference: 12 equivalent protons, one singlet, very shielded (δ 0), inert, volatile, soluble; DSS in D2O.
7. Factor 1, electronegativity: CH3F about 4.3 > CH3Cl 3.1 > CH3Br 2.7 > CH3I 2.2 > CH4 0.2 ppm; effect falls with distance, adds up with more substituents.
8. Factor 2, anisotropy: benzene ring current deshields Ar–H (about 7.3); C=O deshields CHO (9–10); alkyne proton shielded along the axis (2–3).
9. Factor 3, hybridisation (sp² C–H downfield of sp³); factor 4, hydrogen bonding (OH, NH, COOH downfield; vary with concentration, D2O exchange); factor 5, van der Waals deshielding; factor 6, solvent effects.
10. Table of typical shifts: alkyl 0.9–1.5, CH3CO 2.0–2.6, O–CH 3.3–4.5, alkene 4.5–6.5, aromatic 6.5–8.5, CHO 9–10, COOH 10–13 ppm.
questions.question: Explain the principle of NMR spectroscopy. Define chemical shift and discuss the factors affecting it.

questions.answer:
1. Block diagram: superconducting magnet → probe (sample tube, RF coil) ← RF transmitter (pulses); probe → RF receiver → ADC → computer (FT) → display; shim coils and deuterium lock around the probe.
2. Magnet: permanent/electromagnet (60–100 MHz, older) or superconducting solenoid (300–1000 MHz) cooled by liquid helium (about 4 K) with a liquid nitrogen jacket.
3. Shim coils correct field inhomogeneity; field–frequency lock follows the ²H signal of the deuterated solvent and corrects drift.
4. Probe holds the 5 mm tube; sample spun by an air turbine to average the field.
5. RF transmitter gives short intense pulses exciting all nuclei of one kind; receiver records the free induction decay (FID).
6. Computer adds scans (S/N rises with √number of scans) and Fourier-transforms the FID into the frequency spectrum; integrates peaks.
7. CW vs FT: CW slowly sweeps field or frequency; FT gives the whole spectrum per pulse, making ¹³C routine.
8. Sample preparation: 5–20 mg (more for ¹³C) in 0.5–0.7 ml deuterated solvent (CDCl3, DMSO-d6, D2O, CD3OD) with TMS; particle-free, no paramagnetic impurities.
9. Applications: structure elucidation (signals, δ, integration, splitting), identity tests, isomer distinction (cis/trans J, substitution pattern), qNMR purity, impurity and residual solvent work, 2D NMR, MRI, drug–protein binding.
questions.question: Describe the instrumentation of an FT-NMR spectrometer with a block diagram. Add a note on sample preparation and applications of NMR.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: molecules are ionised in the gas phase, ions are separated by m/z under high vacuum and counted; spectrum = relative abundance vs m/z; base peak = 100%.
2. Block diagram: inlet (probe, GC, LC) → ion source → mass analyser → detector (electron multiplier) → data system; vacuum pumps (rotary + turbomolecular).
3. Electron impact: 70 eV electrons from a heated filament; M + e⁻ → M⁺• + 2e⁻; hard ionisation, many reproducible fragments, library searching; M⁺• may be weak.
4. Chemical ionisation: reagent gas (methane, isobutane, ammonia) at about 1 torr; CH4 → CH5⁺; CH5⁺ + M → [M + H]⁺; soft, confirms molecular mass.
5. MALDI: analyte mixed with UV-absorbing matrix (sinapinic acid, CHCA) dried on a plate, pulsed laser desorbs and ionises; mostly [M + H]⁺; proteins and polymers; paired with TOF. (FAB: liquid matrix such as glycerol bombarded with fast Ar/Xe atoms.)
6. Quadrupole: four parallel rods with DC + RF voltages; only one m/z has a stable path at given U and V; scanning U/V passes each m/z; cheap, fast, unit resolution, good for GC-MS and LC-MS/MS.
7. TOF: ions accelerated by voltage V, drift in tube L; t = L√(m/2zeV); light ions arrive first; very wide mass range, fast; reflectron improves resolution. Example: L = 1 m, 20 kV, m/z 1000 arrives in about 16.1 µs.
8. Detector: electron multiplier (dynode cascade, about 10⁶ gain), Faraday cup, microchannel plate.
9. Applications: molecular mass and formula (HRMS), structure from fragments, impurities, metabolites, proteins, isotope studies, forensic analysis.
questions.question: Describe the principle and instrumentation of mass spectrometry. Explain electron impact, chemical ionisation and MALDI, and the quadrupole and time-of-flight analysers.

questions.answer:
1. Coupling: neighbouring non-equivalent protons influence each other's local field through bonding electrons, splitting each other's signals.
2. n + 1 rule: n equivalent neighbours give n + 1 lines; intensities from Pascal's triangle (doublet 1:1, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1).
3. Example ethanol: CH3 triplet (δ about 1.2, 3H), CH2 quartet (about 3.7, 2H), OH broad singlet.
4. Coupling constant J: spacing between lines in Hz; independent of field strength; coupled partners share the same J. Lines at δ 1.262, 1.238, 1.214 on 300 MHz → J = 0.024 × 300 = 7.2 Hz.
5. Typical J: vicinal about 7, trans alkene 12–18, cis 6–12, ortho 6–9, meta 1–3 Hz. Equivalent protons do not split each other.
questions.question: What is spin–spin coupling? Explain the n + 1 rule and coupling constant with an example.

questions.answer:
1. Need: the population excess between α and β is tiny; without return of excited nuclei the signal saturates.
2. Spin–lattice (longitudinal) relaxation, T1: excited nuclei transfer energy to the surroundings (lattice).
3. Spin–spin (transverse) relaxation, T2: exchange of energy between neighbouring spins; loss of phase coherence.
4. Line width ≈ 1/πT2: solids and viscous samples have short T2 → broad lines; liquids give sharp lines.
5. Paramagnetic impurities shorten relaxation and broaden lines; quaternary ¹³C relax slowly, giving small peaks.
questions.question: Write a note on relaxation processes in NMR.

questions.answer:
1. Abundance 99.98% vs 1.1%; ¹³C sensitivity roughly 1/5700 of ¹H, needs FT and many scans.
2. Shift range 0–12 vs 0–220 ppm; C–C coupling not seen in ¹³C; integration reliable for ¹H, not for ¹³C.
3. Broadband (noise) decoupling: irradiating all protons removes C–H splitting, so each different carbon gives a singlet, with NOE enhancement.
4. DEPT-90 shows only CH; DEPT-135 shows CH and CH3 positive, CH2 negative, quaternary absent. Off-resonance gives CH3 quartet, CH2 triplet, CH doublet, C singlet.
5. Typical ¹³C shifts: alkyl 10–50, C–O 50–90, aromatic 100–160, C=O 160–220 ppm.
questions.question: Compare ¹H NMR and ¹³C NMR. Explain broadband decoupling and DEPT.

questions.answer:

Molecular ion carries excess energy and breaks at weak bonds to give stable ions: α-cleavage (acylium ions), benzylic cleavage (tropylium m/z 91 from toluene, M 92), McLafferty rearrangement (γ-H transfer, loss of alkene), loss of small neutrals (H2O 18, CO 28, CO2 44, ketene 42), retro-Diels–Alder.
2. Example acetophenone: M⁺• 120 → loss of CH3• → C6H5CO⁺ 105 (base peak) → loss of CO → C6H5⁺ 77.
3. Nitrogen rule: odd molecular mass = odd number of N atoms.
4. Isotope peaks: M + 1 about 1.1% per carbon; one Cl gives M : M + 2 about 3 : 1 (chlorobenzene 112/114); one Br about 1 : 1; S about 4.4% M + 2.
5. Base peak = most abundant ion; metastable ions = broad weak peaks at non-integer m/z.

1. Principle: measures the difference in heat flow (mW) needed to keep sample and reference on the same temperature programme; peak area = enthalpy change, so it is quantitative.
2. Power-compensation DSC: separate heaters and sensors for sample and reference; controller supplies extra power ΔP = dH/dt to the sample.
3. Heat-flux DSC: one furnace; temperature difference across a disc of known thermal resistance converted to heat flow.
4. Parts: sample and reference pans (aluminium, crimped/hermetic), furnace, temperature programmer, sensors, purge gas (N2), data system. Block diagram with both pans and controller.
5. Curve: endothermic (melting, dehydration) and exothermic (crystallisation, oxidation) peaks; Tg as a baseline step; read onset, peak temperature and area (ΔH, J/g).
6. Calibration: indium (mp 156.6 °C, about 28.5 J/g), zinc, tin; sapphire for heat capacity.
7. Factors: heating rate, sample mass, pan type, purge gas, particle size, thermal history.
8. Applications: polymorphism, purity by van't Hoff (Ts = T0 − RT0²x2/ΔHf × 1/F), drug–excipient compatibility, glass transition of amorphous drugs and solid dispersions, hydrates, freeze-drying design, liposome transitions, protein unfolding.
9. DTA vs DSC: DTA records ΔT (°C), mostly qualitative, reaches very high temperatures; DSC records heat flow (mW), accurate enthalpy, the routine pharmaceutical tool.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: mass of the sample is recorded continuously while it is heated at a controlled rate in a chosen atmosphere; steps show loss of volatiles or decomposition. DTG (dm/dt) turns steps into peaks.
2. Thermobalance: null-point microbalance; electromagnetic restoring force proportional to mass change; kept outside the hot zone.
3. Crucible (platinum, alumina), furnace up to about 1000–1500 °C, temperature programmer and thermocouple, purge gas (N2, air), recorder.
4. Factors: heating rate, sample mass and particle size, atmosphere and flow, crucible shape and material, buoyancy (blank correction), packing, condensation of volatiles.
5. Calcium oxalate monohydrate (Mr 146.1): step 1 loses H2O 12.3% (residue 87.7%), step 2 loses CO 19.2% (CaCO3, 68.5%), step 3 loses CO2 30.1% (CaO, 38.4%).
6. Calculation: % loss = mass of lost molecule/Mr × 100.
7. Applications: water and solvent content, hydrates vs surface moisture (theophylline monohydrate expected 9.1% loss), thermal stability, decomposition temperature, composition of mixtures, ash, decomposition kinetics, polymers and excipients, evolved gas analysis with IR or MS.

questions.answer:
1. X-rays (0.1–100 Å) scatter from electrons; parallel planes spaced d apart reflect at angle θ.
2. Derivation: the lower ray travels an extra path 2d sinθ; constructive interference when the extra path is a whole number of wavelengths: nλ = 2d sinθ.
3. Example: Cu Kα 1.5406 Å, 2θ = 20° → θ = 10° → d = 4.44 Å. NaCl (a = 5.64 Å) d200 = 2.82 Å → 2θ about 31.7°.
4. Rotating crystal: single crystal rotated about one axis in a monochromatic beam; cylindrical film shows layer lines; spacing gives repeat distance and unit cell.
5. Single crystal diffractometer: crystal on goniometer rotated in many orientations; spot positions → unit cell and space group; intensities → structure factors; phase problem solved by direct or Patterson methods; electron-density map; refinement → bond lengths, angles, absolute configuration.
6. Powder method: random crystallites; diffractometer records intensity vs 2θ (Debye–Scherrer camera gives rings); d-values and intensities form a fingerprint; amorphous gives a halo; Scherrer equation for crystallite size.
7. Laue method (white radiation, stationary crystal) for symmetry and orientation.
8. Applications: polymorph and solvate identification, crystallinity and amorphous content, quantitative phase analysis, form changes on processing and storage, 3D structure of drugs and drug–protein complexes, patents on crystal forms, excipient crystallinity.

questions.answer:
1. Coolidge tube: heated tungsten filament emits electrons, accelerated by 30–50 kV onto a water-cooled metal target (Cu, Mo); X-rays leave through beryllium windows.
2. Continuous (bremsstrahlung): electrons decelerate near target nuclei, giving a smooth range; λmin = hc/eV (about 0.41 Å at 30 kV).
3. Characteristic: incoming electron ejects a K-shell electron; L or M electron fills the hole emitting Kα or Kβ of fixed energy (Cu Kα about 1.54 Å, Mo Kα about 0.71 Å).
4. Moseley's law: √ν proportional to atomic number.
5. Monochromatisation: Ni filter removes Cu Kβ; crystal monochromator; detectors: counters, scintillation, area detectors.

questions.answer:
1. Crystal: regular 3D repeating arrangement; amorphous solid lacks long-range order.
2. Unit cell: smallest repeating unit with edges a, b, c and angles α, β, γ.
3. Seven crystal systems (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal, rhombohedral) and fourteen Bravais lattices; most drugs are monoclinic, triclinic or orthorhombic.
4. Miller indices (hkl): reciprocals of the plane's intercepts on the axes, cleared of fractions; for cubic cells d = a/√(h² + k² + l²).
5. Polymorphism and pseudopolymorphism (hydrates, solvates) change melting point, solubility and bioavailability.

questions.answer:
1. Validation: documented evidence giving a high degree of assurance that a method or process consistently produces results meeting predetermined specifications. ICH Q2(R1)/Q2(R2); US FDA guidance (2015) on analytical procedures.
2. Specificity: unequivocal measurement in presence of impurities, degradants, matrix; placebo, forced degradation, peak purity, resolution.
3. Accuracy: closeness to true value; % recovery from spiked placebo; at least 9 determinations at 3 levels (80, 100, 120%). Example 9.87 of 10.00 mg → 98.7%.
4. Precision: repeatability (same conditions; 9 determinations or 6 at 100%), intermediate precision (days, analysts, instruments), reproducibility (between labs). Example six results → RSD 0.64%.
5. LOD = 3.3σ/S (S/N about 3); LOQ = 10σ/S (S/N about 10). Example σ 0.0021, S 0.052 → LOD 0.13, LOQ 0.40 µg/ml.
6. Linearity: at least 5 concentrations; regression, r, slope, intercept, residuals.
7. Range: assay 80–120%, content uniformity 70–130%, dissolution ±20%, impurities reporting level to 120% of limit.
8. Robustness: small deliberate changes in pH, mobile phase ratio, flow, temperature, column lot.
9. Table of which parameters apply to identification, impurity (quantitative/limit) and assay; system suitability (resolution, tailing, plates, RSD of injections).

questions.answer:
1. Purpose: assays depend on correct wavelength and absorbance scale; required by GMP (21 CFR 211.160, Schedule M) with SOP, frequency and records.
2. UV wavelength control: holmium perchlorate (241.15, 287.15, 361.5, 536.3 nm), holmium glass, mercury lines, deuterium lines 486.0 and 656.1 nm; tolerance ±1 nm UV, ±3 nm visible.
3. UV absorbance control: potassium dichromate (dried at 130 °C, about 57–63 mg in 0.005 M H2SO4 to 1000 ml); A(1%, 1 cm) at 235, 257, 313, 350 nm about 124.5, 144.5, 48.6, 106.6 within pharmacopoeial ranges.
4. Stray light: 1.2% w/v KCl, absorbance > 2.0 at about 200 nm.
5. Resolution: 0.02% v/v toluene in hexane, ratio A(about 269 nm)/A(about 266 nm) at least 1.5.
6. Cells matched, clean; baseline flatness, noise, drift.
7. IR wavenumber accuracy: polystyrene film (about 35 µm); bands 3060.0, 2849.5, 1942.9, 1601.2, 1583.0, 1154.5, 1028.3 cm⁻¹ within tolerance.
8. IR resolution: trough depths between 2870 and 2849.5 cm⁻¹ and between 1589 and 1583 cm⁻¹; 100% line, noise, energy throughput; dry atmosphere (avoid H2O and CO2 bands).
9. Record results, label status, act on failure (remove, investigate, repair, recalibrate).

1. Definition and importance: measurement of an antigen by competition with radiolabelled antigen for limited antibody sites; Yalow and Berson (insulin, about 1959–1960); pg–ng sensitivity, high specificity.
2. Principle: law of mass action; Ag* + Ab ⇌ Ag*Ab and Ag + Ab ⇌ AgAb; fixed Ag* and limited Ab; more sample Ag → less bound radioactivity (inverse relation).
3. Components: antigen standards; tracer (¹²⁵I gamma about 60 days, ³H beta about 12.3 years; iodination by chloramine-T, lactoperoxidase, Bolton–Hunter); specific antibody (titre, affinity, specificity; haptens coupled to carrier protein); buffer; separation system; gamma or liquid scintillation counter.
4. Procedure: pipette standards/samples, add tracer and antibody, incubate to equilibrium, separate bound from free, count the bound fraction.
5. Standard curve: B/B0 (%) vs log concentration, sigmoid; logit–log linear; example B0 8000 of 20,000 cpm, sample 4000 → B/B0 50%.
6. Controls: total counts, NSB, zero standard, QC samples, duplicates.
7. Limitations: radiation hazard and licensing, waste disposal, short tracer life, expensive counters, cross-reactivity, antibody production, long incubations.
8. Applications: hormones (insulin, T3, T4, TSH, steroids, hCG), therapeutic drug monitoring (digoxin), pharmacokinetics, drugs of abuse, tumour markers (CEA, AFP, PSA), vitamin B12, folate, viral antigens.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: miniature column chromatography; analyte retained on solid sorbent from liquid sample, interferences washed off, analyte eluted with small volume of strong solvent.
2. Steps: conditioning (methanol), equilibration (water/buffer, do not dry), sample loading, washing (weak solvent), elution (strong solvent); evaporate and reconstitute. Diagram of cartridge with frits and sorbent.
3. Sorbents: reversed phase (C18, C8, polymeric), normal phase (silica, alumina, Florisil, diol, CN, NH2), ion exchange (SCX, SAX, weak), mixed mode.
4. Formats: cartridges, disks, 96-well plates, pipette tips, SPME fibres.
5. Terms: capacity, breakthrough volume, recovery, concentration factor.
6. Applications: plasma/urine bioanalysis before LC-MS/MS, trace pollutants, herbal clean-up, desalting peptides.
7. Comparison with LLE: solvent use small vs large; no emulsions vs emulsions common; high selectivity and concentration; easy automation; better reproducibility; cartridges cost more; LLE uses simple equipment.

questions.answer:
1. Nernst distribution law: K = C(organic)/C(aqueous) at constant temperature for the same species.
2. Distribution ratio D includes ionised forms; weak acid D = K/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)): acids extracted from acidic, bases from alkaline solution. pKa 4.5 acid: 99% un-ionised at pH 2.5, 0.1% at pH 7.5.
3. Solvent choice: immiscible, selective, suitable density (CHCl3, DCM lower layer; ether, ethyl acetate, hexane upper), volatile, safe, peroxide-free.
4. Multiple extraction: q(n) = [Vaq/(D·Vorg + Vaq)]ⁿ. D = 4, Vaq 50 ml: one 30 ml extraction removes 70.6%; three 10 ml extractions remove 82.9%.
5. Procedure with separating funnel: adjust pH, salting out, shake and vent, separate, repeat, combine, dry over anhydrous Na2SO4, evaporate, reconstitute.
6. Back-extraction for clean-up; emulsion remedies (centrifuge, salt, glass wool).
7. Variants: continuous extraction, Soxhlet, ion-pair extraction, supported liquid extraction, microextraction.
8. Advantages and disadvantages; uses in drug isolation from plasma and plant material.

1. Principle: HPLC separates; eluate ionised at atmospheric pressure; ions pass into a triple quadrupole for MS/MS.
2. Interface problem: 1 ml of eluent gives more than a litre of vapour; solved by atmospheric pressure ionisation (old: moving belt, thermospray, particle beam).
3. ESI: high voltage (2–5 kV) capillary, Taylor cone, charged droplets, desolvation by heated gas, Coulomb fission at Rayleigh limit, gas-phase ions; [M + H]⁺, [M − H]⁻; multiply charged proteins (15,000 Da with 10 H⁺ → m/z about 1501).
4. APCI: heated nebuliser (350–500 °C) vaporises eluent; corona discharge ionises solvent; proton transfer to analyte; singly charged; less polar compounds; higher flows.
5. Instrumentation: pump, autosampler, column, source, ion optics, Q1 (precursor) → q2 collision cell (CID with Ar/N2) → Q3 (product) → electron multiplier → data system; diagram.
6. Scan modes: product ion, precursor ion, neutral loss, MRM; paracetamol 152 → 110.
7. Practical rules: volatile buffers (formic acid, ammonium formate/acetate), no phosphate; stable-isotope internal standard; clean-up to reduce ion suppression.

questions.answer:

3. Interface: capillary column directly into ion source via heated transfer line; for packed columns separators—jet (He diffuses away from supersonic jet), effusion (porous glass), membrane (silicone).
4. Ion source EI 70 eV (library spectra) or CI; analyser quadrupole, ion trap, TOF; triple quadrupole for GC-MS/MS; electron multiplier; vacuum pumps.
5. Data: TIC, mass spectrum of each peak with library search, EIC, SIM for quantitation, MRM in GC-MS/MS.
6. Derivatisation: silylation, acylation, methylation for polar drugs.
7. Advantages and limitations (volatile/thermally stable compounds only).
8. Applications: residual solvents (headspace), forensic toxicology and drugs of abuse, doping, pesticide residues, essential oils, volatile/genotoxic impurities, environmental analysis, metabolomics.

questions.answer:

2. Energy: high voltage on capillary vs heated nebuliser (350–500 °C) + corona needle.
3. Analytes: ESI polar, ionic, large (peptides, proteins); APCI medium/low polarity, small, thermally stable (steroids).
4. Charges: ESI multiply charged ions; APCI singly charged.

1. Separation and identification in one run without collecting fractions (GC-MS of essential oils).
2. Two independent identification criteria (retention + mass) → high selectivity (MRM in plasma).
3. High sensitivity to pg/ml (LC-MS/MS bioanalysis).
4. Structural information on unknowns (impurity and metabolite identification).

questions.question: Write the advantages of hyphenated techniques with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Need: GC carrier gas flow vs MS high vacuum; remove carrier gas, keep analyte.
2. Direct capillary interface: column end inserted into source via heated transfer line; about 1 ml/min He handled by pumps.
3. Jet separator: supersonic jet; light helium diffuses sideways and is pumped off; heavier analyte enters next nozzle.
4. Effusion (Watson–Biemann) separator: porous glass tube, helium effuses through pores.
5. Membrane separator: silicone membrane lets organic molecules pass, holds back helium.
questions.question: Describe the interfaces used in GC-MS.

questions.answer:
1. Volatile additives only: formic acid, acetic acid, ammonium formate/acetate, ammonia.
2. Avoid non-volatile buffers (phosphate, sulfate) and non-volatile ion-pair reagents; they deposit in the source and suppress signals.
3. Low flow rates or flow splitting; narrow-bore/UHPLC columns.
4. Clean samples (SPE, LLE, protein precipitation) to limit matrix effects.
5. Stable-isotope-labelled internal standard to correct ion suppression and losses.

# Unit 1: NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry

UV and IR spectra (studied in BP701T) tell you that a molecule has a chromophore or a carbonyl group. They rarely tell you how the atoms are joined. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) maps the hydrogen and carbon skeleton atom by atom, and mass spectrometry (MS) weighs the molecule and its pieces. Together they are the two main tools for proving the structure of a new drug, an impurity or a metabolite. This unit covers the theory, the instruments and the uses of both.

## 1.1 Principle of NMR

Some atomic nuclei spin. A spinning charge behaves like a tiny bar magnet with a **nuclear spin quantum number (I)**.

| Nucleus | I | Natural abundance | NMR active? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ¹H | 1/2 | about 99.98% | Yes, most sensitive |
| ¹³C | 1/2 | about 1.1% | Yes, weak signal |
| ¹⁹F, ³¹P | 1/2 | 100% | Yes |
| ²H (deuterium) | 1 | about 0.015% | Yes, used for the lock |
| ¹²C, ¹⁶O | 0 | major isotopes | No (no spin) |

Rule: a nucleus with an even number of protons **and** an even number of neutrons has I = 0 and gives no NMR signal. That is why ¹²C and ¹⁶O are "invisible" and organic spectra show only ¹H or ¹³C.

**In a magnetic field.** A nucleus with I = 1/2 can take 2I + 1 = 2 orientations in an external field B0:

```text
 Energy
   ^                     β (spin -1/2, against the field)  ---------
   |                                                          ^
   |        no field: one level         ΔE = hν = γhB0/2π     |  absorb radio waves
   |        ------------------                                |
   |                     α (spin +1/2, with the field)    ---------
   +------------------------------------------------------------> field B0
 The gap ΔE grows in direct proportion to B0.
```

The nucleus also **precesses** around the field direction, like a spinning top, at the **Larmor frequency**:

**ν = γB0 / 2π**

where γ is the magnetogyric (gyromagnetic) ratio, a constant for each nucleus. When radio-frequency radiation of exactly this frequency is applied, nuclei flip from α to β: this is **resonance**. A 7.05 T magnet gives about 300 MHz for ¹H and about 75 MHz for ¹³C; a 9.4 T magnet gives about 400 MHz for ¹H and 100 MHz for ¹³C. Spectrometers are named by their ¹H frequency ("a 400 MHz NMR").

**Why NMR is insensitive.** The energy gap is tiny, so the two levels are almost equally filled (Boltzmann distribution). At 300 MHz and 25 °C, the ratio of upper to lower population is about 0.99995: for every million nuclei in the upper level there are only about 1,000,048 in the lower level. Only this small excess gives a signal, which is why NMR needs milligram amounts and stronger magnets give better spectra.

## 1.2 Relaxation

After absorbing energy, nuclei must return to the lower level, or the small excess disappears and the signal fades (**saturation**). Two relaxation processes do this:

| Process | Also called | What happens | Symbol |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spin–lattice relaxation | Longitudinal relaxation | Excited nuclei hand energy to the surroundings (the "lattice": solvent and other molecules) | T1 |
| Spin–spin relaxation | Transverse relaxation | Nuclei exchange spin energy with neighbouring nuclei; the precessing spins lose phase coherence | T2 |

- Liquids: T1 and T2 are about 0.1 to several seconds, so lines are sharp.
- Solids and viscous samples: T2 is very short, so lines are very broad. This is why routine NMR is done in solution.
- Line width ≈ 1/(πT2): fast relaxation gives broad lines (uncertainty principle).
- Paramagnetic impurities (O2, metal ions) shorten relaxation and broaden lines.
- ¹³C nuclei without attached H (quaternary carbons) relax slowly, so their peaks are small.

## 1.3 Chemical shift

If every proton resonated at exactly γB0/2π, all would give one line and NMR would be useless. In a molecule, the electrons circulating around a nucleus create a small field that opposes B0. The nucleus feels a slightly smaller field:

**B(effective) = B0 (1 − σ)**, where σ is the shielding constant.

- **Shielded** proton: more electron density, resonates at higher field (lower frequency), to the **right** of the spectrum (upfield).
- **Deshielded** proton: less electron density, resonates at lower field, to the **left** (downfield).

Because the frequency difference depends on the magnet, the position is expressed in a field-independent unit, the **chemical shift δ** in parts per million:

**δ (ppm) = [ν(sample) − ν(TMS)] / ν(spectrometer) × 10⁶**

**Reference: tetramethylsilane (TMS), Si(CH3)4,** is set at δ 0 because:

1. All 12 protons are equivalent and give one sharp singlet.
2. Silicon is less electronegative than carbon, so its protons are more shielded than almost all organic protons; the TMS peak sits at the right edge, clear of others.
3. It is chemically inert, non-polar, soluble in most organic solvents and volatile (bp about 27 °C), so it is easy to remove.
4. In water (D2O), the water-soluble salt DSS (sodium 2,2-dimethyl-2-silapentane-5-sulfonate) is used instead.

**Worked example.** On a 300 MHz instrument a signal appears 2190 Hz downfield from TMS.
δ = 2190/300 = **7.30 ppm** (a benzene-ring proton). On a 400 MHz instrument the same proton appears 7.30 × 400 = 2920 Hz from TMS, but δ is still 7.30 ppm. That is the point of using ppm.

**Typical ¹H chemical shifts**

| Proton type | δ (ppm) |
| --- | --- |
| TMS | 0 |
| Alkyl C–H (CH3, CH2) | 0.9–1.5 |
| CH3 next to C=O (CH3–CO) | 2.0–2.6 |
| CH3 on a benzene ring | about 2.3 |
| Alkyne ≡C–H | 2–3 |
| H–C–O (alcohol, ether, ester O–CH) | 3.3–4.5 |
| Alkene =C–H | 4.5–6.5 |
| Aromatic Ar–H | 6.5–8.5 |
| Aldehyde CHO | 9–10 |
| Carboxylic acid COOH | 10–13 |
| Alcohol OH, amine NH | variable, about 1–5 (depends on concentration and H-bonding) |

## 1.4 Factors affecting chemical shift

1. **Electronegativity (inductive effect).** An electronegative atom pulls electron density away and deshields nearby protons. Methyl halides show this neatly: CH3F about 4.3, CH3Cl about 3.1, CH3Br about 2.7, CH3I about 2.2 and CH4 about 0.2 ppm. The effect weakens quickly with distance and adds up (CH2Cl2 and CHCl3 move further downfield).
2. **Magnetic anisotropy (π-electron circulation).** π electrons circulate in the field and set up their own field that shields some regions and deshields others.
   - Benzene ring current deshields the ring protons (δ about 7.3).
   - The C=O group deshields an aldehyde proton (δ 9–10).
   - Alkene protons are deshielded (δ 4.5–6.5).
   - The cylinder of π electrons in an alkyne shields the acetylenic proton along the axis (δ only 2–3, upfield of alkenes).
3. **Hybridisation.** sp² carbons hold electrons closer, so attached protons are deshielded compared with sp³ C–H.
4. **Hydrogen bonding.** H-bonded protons (OH, NH, COOH) are deshielded; their shift moves with concentration, temperature and solvent. Intramolecular H-bonds (for example in salicylic acid) give a large downfield shift that does not change on dilution.
5. **Van der Waals deshielding.** Crowded protons squeezed by nearby groups move slightly downfield.
6. **Solvent effects.** Aromatic solvents such as benzene-d6 shift signals by their own anisotropy.
7. **Exchange.** OH and NH protons exchange with D2O; adding a drop of D2O makes their signal disappear (the D2O exchange test).

## 1.5 Spin–spin coupling and coupling constant

Neighbouring non-equivalent protons influence each other's local field through the bonding electrons. Each proton "sees" the spin states of the protons on the next carbon, so its signal splits. This is **spin–spin coupling**.

**The n + 1 rule (first-order spectra).** A proton with n equivalent neighbouring protons is split into n + 1 lines. The relative intensities follow Pascal's triangle.

```text
 Neighbours (n)   Lines   Name        Intensities
      0             1     singlet     1
      1             2     doublet     1 : 1
      2             3     triplet     1 : 2 : 1
      3             4     quartet     1 : 3 : 3 : 1
      4             5     quintet     1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1
      6             7     septet      1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1
```

**Example: ethanol, CH3–CH2–OH (in pure dry sample, ignoring OH coupling).**
- CH3 (δ about 1.2): neighbours are the 2 CH2 protons → triplet, integrating 3H.
- CH2 (δ about 3.7): neighbours are 3 CH3 protons → quartet, integrating 2H.
- OH: a broad singlet, position variable (fast exchange removes its coupling).

**Example: ethyl acetate, CH3COOCH2CH3.** Acetyl CH3 singlet near 2.0 (3H), O–CH2 quartet near 4.1 (2H), CH3 triplet near 1.3 (3H).

**Coupling constant (J)** is the distance between two adjacent lines of a multiplet, in hertz.

- J does **not** change with the magnet strength (δ in Hz does), so a 300 MHz and a 600 MHz spectrum give the same J.
- Protons that couple to each other share the same J. Matching J values tells you which groups are neighbours.
- Worked example: a triplet on a 300 MHz spectrum has lines at δ 1.262, 1.238 and 1.214. Spacing = 0.024 ppm × 300 = **7.2 Hz**, a typical free-rotating CH2–CH3 coupling.

| Coupling type | Typical J (Hz) |
| --- | --- |
| Vicinal H–C–C–H, free rotation | about 6–8 |
| Alkene, trans | about 12–18 |
| Alkene, cis | about 6–12 |
| Geminal on an sp² carbon (=CH2) | 0–3 |
| Aromatic ortho | 6–9 |
| Aromatic meta | 1–3 |
| Aromatic para | 0–1 |

**Rules.**
- Equivalent protons do not split each other (the CH3 of ethane is one singlet).
- Coupling normally reaches over three bonds (H–C–C–H); weaker long-range coupling can appear in alkenes and aromatics.
- When the shift difference between two groups (Δν in Hz) is not much larger than J, the spectrum becomes **second order**: line intensities lean towards each other ("roof effect") and the simple n + 1 rule fails. Higher-field magnets increase Δν and simplify such spectra.

**Integration.** The area under each signal is proportional to the number of protons giving it. The instrument draws a step curve; the ratio of step heights gives the proton ratio (3 : 2 : 1 for ethanol).

## 1.6 ¹³C NMR

**Differences from ¹H NMR**

| Feature | ¹H NMR | ¹³C NMR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural abundance | about 99.98% | about 1.1% |
| Relative sensitivity | 1 | very low (roughly 1/5700 of ¹H at natural abundance) |
| Shift range | about 0–12 ppm | about 0–220 ppm |
| Frequency at 9.4 T | 400 MHz | about 100 MHz |
| C–C coupling | — | not seen (two ¹³C atoms are rarely next to each other) |
| Integration | reliable | not reliable (slow relaxation, NOE) |
| Sample and time | a few mg, minutes | more sample, many scans (FT essential) |

**Proton-decoupled spectra.** ¹³C couples strongly to attached protons. In routine spectra the protons are irradiated with a broad band of radio frequency (**broadband or noise decoupling**), which removes all C–H splitting. Each chemically different carbon then gives **one singlet**. Decoupling also increases peak heights through the **nuclear Overhauser effect (NOE)**.

**Off-resonance decoupling** (older) and **DEPT** (distortionless enhancement by polarisation transfer) show how many H atoms each carbon carries:

| Experiment | CH3 | CH2 | CH | Quaternary C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Off-resonance (n + 1 rule on directly bonded H) | quartet | triplet | doublet | singlet |
| DEPT-90 | absent | absent | positive | absent |
| DEPT-135 | positive | negative (inverted) | positive | absent |

**Typical ¹³C shifts**

| Carbon type | δ (ppm) |
| --- | --- |
| Alkyl CH3, CH2, CH | 10–50 |
| C–N | 30–65 |
| C–O (alcohol, ether) | 50–90 |
| Alkyne C≡C | 65–90 |
| Alkene and aromatic | 100–160 |
| Nitrile C≡N | 110–125 |
| Ester, acid, amide C=O | 160–185 |
| Aldehyde, ketone C=O | 190–220 |

Common solvent: CDCl3, whose residual CHCl3 shows at δ 7.26 in ¹H spectra and whose carbon gives a small triplet near δ 77 in ¹³C spectra (C–D coupling, deuterium I = 1 gives 2nI + 1 = 3 lines).

## 1.7 Instrumentation of NMR

Modern instruments are **pulsed Fourier transform (FT-NMR)** spectrometers. Older **continuous-wave (CW)** instruments swept the field or frequency slowly and took several minutes per spectrum.

```text
                 +------------------- Computer (pulse control, FT, display) ----------+
                 |                                                                    |
        RF transmitter (pulse) ----> probe coil around sample <---- RF receiver ----> ADC
                                         |   (sample tube, spun)       (FID)
                 Superconducting magnet: [ N ]  sample in probe  [ S ]
                 Shim coils (field homogeneity)   Lock channel (2H of solvent)
```

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| **Magnet** | Strong, stable, uniform field. Permanent or electromagnets (60–100 MHz, old); **superconducting** solenoid (300–1000 MHz) kept at about 4 K in liquid helium, with a liquid nitrogen jacket to slow helium loss |
| **Shim coils** | Small extra coils that correct field unevenness across the sample; good shimming gives sharp lines |
| **Field–frequency lock** | Monitors the deuterium signal of the solvent and corrects any drift of the field |
| **Sample probe** | Holds the 5 mm glass tube in the centre of the field; contains the transmitter/receiver coil; air turbine spins the tube (about 20 Hz) to average field differences |
| **RF transmitter** | Gives short, intense pulses (microseconds) that excite all nuclei of one kind at once |
| **RF receiver and detector** | Picks up the decaying signal emitted by the nuclei, the **free induction decay (FID)** |
| **Computer** | Adds many scans to improve signal-to-noise (S/N rises with the square root of the number of scans), performs the **Fourier transform** (time domain → frequency domain spectrum), integrates and prints |

**Sample preparation.** About 5–20 mg (more for ¹³C) dissolved in about 0.5–0.7 ml of a deuterated solvent (CDCl3, DMSO-d6, D2O, CD3OD) with a little TMS. Deuterated solvents avoid a huge solvent proton peak and provide the lock signal. The solution must be free of solid particles and paramagnetic impurities.

**FT advantage.** One pulse excites the whole spectrum; a spectrum is collected every few seconds; hundreds of scans can be averaged. This made ¹³C NMR routine.

## 1.8 Applications of NMR

1. **Structure elucidation** of new drugs, natural products, metabolites and degradation products: number of proton types (number of signals), their environment (δ), ratio (integration) and neighbours (splitting, J).
2. **Identification and identity tests:** comparison with a reference spectrum.
3. **Distinguishing isomers:** cis/trans alkenes (J), ortho/meta/para substitution patterns, keto–enol tautomers.
4. **Quantitative NMR (qNMR):** signal area is proportional to the number of nuclei, so purity or content can be found against an internal standard of known purity without a reference standard of the analyte.
5. **Impurity profiling** and checking residual solvents.
6. **Hydrogen bonding and exchange studies** (D2O shake, temperature effects).
7. **Two-dimensional NMR** (COSY, HSQC, HMBC) to connect protons and carbons in complex molecules.
8. **Medical imaging:** magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses the same principle on water protons in tissue.
9. **Drug–protein binding and conformation** studies.

## 1.9 Principle of mass spectrometry

A mass spectrometer **turns molecules into gaseous ions, separates the ions by their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and counts them**. It does not use radiation; strictly it is not "spectroscopy", but the plot of ion abundance against m/z is called the mass spectrum.

```text
 Sample inlet ──> Ion source ──> Mass analyser ──> Detector ──> Data system
  (probe, GC,     (EI, CI, ESI,   (quadrupole,      (electron
   LC, plate)      FAB, MALDI)     TOF, magnetic)    multiplier)
                 └────────────── all under high vacuum ──────────────┘
```

**Terms used on a mass spectrum**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| m/z | Mass of the ion divided by its charge; for singly charged ions, m/z = mass |
| Molecular ion (M⁺•) | The molecule minus one electron: a radical cation whose m/z gives the molecular mass |
| Base peak | The tallest peak, set to 100% relative abundance; all others are scaled to it |
| Fragment ions | Smaller ions formed when M⁺• breaks |
| Isotope peaks | M + 1, M + 2 peaks from heavier isotopes (¹³C, ³⁷Cl, ⁸¹Br, ³⁴S) |
| Metastable ions | Ions that break up on the way through the analyser; broad, weak peaks at non-integer m/z |
| Quasi-molecular ion | [M + H]⁺ or [M − H]⁻ formed by soft ionisation |

**High vacuum** (about 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷ torr in the analyser) is needed so that ions do not collide with air molecules before reaching the detector.

## 1.10 Ionisation techniques

| Technique | How ions form | Type | Suits | Main ion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Electron impact (EI)** | Vapour hit by a beam of 70 eV electrons from a heated filament | Hard | Volatile, thermally stable, small molecules (GC-MS) | M⁺• plus many fragments |
| **Chemical ionisation (CI)** | Reagent gas (methane, isobutane, ammonia) ionised by electrons; reagent ions (CH5⁺) transfer a proton to the sample | Soft | Molecules whose M⁺• is weak in EI | [M + H]⁺, little fragmentation |
| **Fast atom bombardment (FAB)** | Sample in a liquid matrix (glycerol, m-nitrobenzyl alcohol) hit by fast neutral atoms (Ar or Xe) | Soft | Polar, non-volatile, larger molecules (peptides, antibiotics, salts) | [M + H]⁺, [M + Na]⁺; matrix peaks |
| **MALDI** (matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation) | Sample mixed with a UV-absorbing matrix (sinapinic acid, α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid), dried on a plate and fired with a pulsed UV laser | Very soft | Proteins, peptides, polymers, oligonucleotides up to very high mass | Mostly singly charged [M + H]⁺; usually with TOF |
| Electrospray (ESI) and APCI | Covered under LC-MS in Unit 5 | Soft | LC-MS | [M + H]⁺, multiply charged ions |

**Electron impact in more detail.** Electrons from a hot tungsten or rhenium filament are accelerated through 70 V towards an anode (trap). Vapour molecules crossing the beam lose an electron: M + e⁻ → M⁺• + 2e⁻. About 10–15 eV is enough to ionise; the extra energy breaks bonds, giving a reproducible "fingerprint" of fragments. Repeller and accelerating plates push the ions into the analyser. Spectra at 70 eV are standard, so library searching is possible.

**Chemical ionisation.** Reagent gas at about 1 torr is ionised: CH4 → CH4⁺• → (with more CH4) CH5⁺ + CH3•. Then CH5⁺ + M → [M + H]⁺ + CH4. The [M + H]⁺ ion carries little excess energy, so it survives. Use CI to confirm the molecular mass when EI gives no M⁺•.

**MALDI.** The matrix absorbs the laser energy and vaporises, carrying the analyte with it and passing protons to it. Because ions are produced in pulses, MALDI pairs naturally with a time-of-flight analyser (MALDI-TOF).

## 1.11 Fragmentation

The molecular ion has extra energy and breaks at its weakest bonds and to give the most stable ions. Common patterns:

1. **α-cleavage:** bond next to a heteroatom or carbonyl breaks, giving a resonance-stabilised cation. Ketones lose an alkyl radical to give an acylium ion (R–C≡O⁺).
2. **Benzylic cleavage:** alkylbenzenes give m/z 91, the very stable **tropylium ion** C7H7⁺ (toluene, M 92, base peak 91).
3. **McLafferty rearrangement:** carbonyl compounds with a γ-hydrogen transfer that hydrogen to the carbonyl oxygen through a six-membered transition state and split off a neutral alkene.
4. **Loss of small neutral molecules:** H2O (18) from alcohols, CO (28) from aldehydes and phenols, CO2 (44) from acids, NH3 (17), HCN (27), ketene CH2=C=O (42) from acetanilides.
5. **Retro-Diels–Alder** cleavage of cyclohexene rings.
6. Stevenson's rule: when a bond breaks, the positive charge stays on the fragment with the lower ionisation energy.

**Worked example: acetophenone, C6H5COCH3 (M = 120).**
- M⁺• at m/z 120.
- α-cleavage loses CH3• (15): C6H5CO⁺ at **m/z 105** (base peak, benzoyl cation).
- Loss of CO (28) from m/z 105 gives C6H5⁺ at **m/z 77** (phenyl cation).

**Isotope patterns and useful rules**

| Rule | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Nitrogen rule | A molecule with an odd molecular mass contains an odd number of N atoms; even mass means zero or an even number of N |
| M + 1 peak | About 1.1% of M for each carbon (from ¹³C); C8 compound: about 8.8% |
| Chlorine | One Cl gives M and M + 2 in about 3 : 1 ratio (³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl); chlorobenzene shows m/z 112 and 114 |
| Bromine | One Br gives M and M + 2 in about 1 : 1 ratio (⁷⁹Br : ⁸¹Br) |
| Sulfur | M + 2 about 4.4% per S (³⁴S) |
| Degree of unsaturation | (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2 rings plus double bonds, from the formula |

**High-resolution MS** measures m/z to four decimal places. Because exact atomic masses are not whole numbers (¹H 1.0078, ¹⁶O 15.9949, ¹⁴N 14.0031), the exact mass fixes the molecular formula. Example: paracetamol C8H9NO2 has nominal mass 151 and monoisotopic mass 151.0633; its protonated ion [M + H]⁺ is m/z 152.0706.

**Resolution (R) = m/Δm**, where Δm is the smallest mass difference that can be separated at mass m. Separating m/z 500.0 from 500.5 needs R = 500/0.5 = 1000.

## 1.12 Mass analysers

### Quadrupole

```text
        rod A (+)          Ions enter along the axis
   ion  ===========  ──>  only ions of one chosen m/z have a stable path
  beam  ===========        and reach the detector; others spiral out
        rod B (−)          and hit the rods
   Four parallel rods: opposite pairs joined; DC voltage + RF voltage applied
```

- Four parallel metal rods; one opposite pair carries +(U + V cos ωt), the other −(U + V cos ωt), where U is a DC voltage and V cos ωt a radio-frequency voltage.
- For a given U and V, only ions of one m/z oscillate stably and pass through; all others collide with the rods. The quadrupole is a **mass filter**.
- Scanning U and V together (keeping U/V constant) brings each m/z through in turn.
- Advantages: small, cheap, fast scanning, tolerant of higher pressure, easy to couple with GC and LC; ideal for selected ion monitoring.
- Limitations: unit resolution only; mass range up to a few thousand.
- A **triple quadrupole** (Q1–q2–Q3) is used for MS/MS (Unit 5).

### Time of flight (TOF)

All ions are given the same kinetic energy by an accelerating voltage V and then drift through a field-free tube of length L:

zeV = ½mv², so the flight time **t = L √(m / 2zeV)**. Heavier ions are slower.

```text
 pulsed ion source ──> accelerating grid (V) ──> field-free drift tube (L) ──> detector
                         light ions arrive first ............ heavy ions arrive last
 Reflectron: an ion mirror at the end that corrects small energy spreads and improves resolution
```

- Worked example: L = 1.0 m, V = 20 kV, singly charged ions. m/z 1000 arrives in about 16.1 µs; m/z 500 in about 11.4 µs; m/z 1001 only about 0.008 µs after m/z 1000. Fast electronics are therefore essential.
- Advantages: practically unlimited mass range (proteins), very fast, whole spectrum from every pulse, high sensitivity; best partner for MALDI.
- Limitation: needs pulsed ionisation; resolution depends on energy spread (improved by the reflectron and delayed extraction).

| Feature | Quadrupole | Time of flight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Separation by | Stability of path in DC + RF field | Flight time in drift tube |
| Mode | Scanning filter | All ions per pulse |
| Mass range | Up to about a few thousand | Very large |
| Resolution | Unit | High (with reflectron) |
| Common partners | EI, CI, ESI; GC-MS, LC-MS/MS | MALDI, ESI (Q-TOF) |

Other analysers met in books: magnetic sector (ions bent in a magnetic field, radius depends on m/z; double-focusing with an electrostatic sector gives high resolution), ion trap, and Orbitrap.

## 1.13 Instrumentation of a mass spectrometer

| Component | Details |
| --- | --- |
| **Sample inlet** | Batch inlet for gases and volatile liquids; direct insertion probe for solids; GC or LC interface; MALDI plate |
| **Ion source** | EI, CI, FAB, MALDI, ESI or APCI (above) |
| **Mass analyser** | Quadrupole, TOF, magnetic sector, ion trap |
| **Detector** | **Electron multiplier** (ion strikes a dynode, releases electrons, which cascade down a series of dynodes, giving about 10⁶ gain); Faraday cup (collects charge directly, very accurate but less sensitive); microchannel plate (TOF) |
| **Vacuum system** | Rotary pump (rough vacuum) plus turbomolecular or diffusion pump (high vacuum) |
| **Data system** | Records m/z and intensity, normalises to base peak, compares with libraries |

## 1.14 Applications of mass spectrometry

1. **Molecular mass** from M⁺• or [M + H]⁺; **molecular formula** from exact mass (HRMS) and isotope pattern.
2. **Structure elucidation** from fragmentation, with NMR and IR.
3. **Identification of impurities and degradation products** at trace levels.
4. **Drug metabolism and pharmacokinetics:** metabolites and plasma drug levels (LC-MS/MS).
5. **Proteins and peptides:** molecular mass of biologics, peptide mapping and sequencing (MALDI-TOF, ESI).
6. **Isotope ratio and labelling studies** (¹³C, ²H, ¹⁵N tracers).
7. **Forensic and doping analysis,** drugs of abuse, pesticide residues (GC-MS).
8. **Microbial identification** by MALDI-TOF protein fingerprints.

## Remember

- ν = γB0/2π; δ = (ν sample − ν TMS)/ν spectrometer × 10⁶; TMS = δ 0.
- Deshielding (electronegative atoms, ring current, H-bonding) moves signals downfield (left).
- n + 1 rule with Pascal's triangle; J in Hz does not change with field strength.
- T1 spin–lattice, T2 spin–spin; short T2 means broad lines.
- ¹³C: 1.1% abundance, 0–220 ppm, broadband decoupled singlets; DEPT-135: CH2 down, CH and CH3 up, quaternary absent.
- MS: ions separated by m/z under high vacuum; base peak = 100%.
- EI is hard (70 eV); CI, FAB and MALDI are soft and give [M + H]⁺.
- Quadrupole = DC + RF mass filter; TOF: t = L√(m/2zeV), light ions arrive first.
- Nitrogen rule; Cl 3 : 1 and Br 1 : 1 M/M + 2; tropylium m/z 91; acetophenone 120 → 105 → 77.

# Unit 2: Thermal methods of analysis and X-ray diffraction

Two batches of the same drug can have the same chemical formula and the same assay value and still behave differently in a tablet, because their solid form differs: one may be a hydrate, another a different polymorph, a third partly amorphous. Thermal methods watch what a solid does when it is heated, and X-ray diffraction looks directly at how its molecules are packed. Both are core tools of preformulation and solid-state quality control.

## 2.1 Thermal methods: the common idea

**Thermal analysis** is a group of techniques in which a property of the sample is measured while its temperature is changed (or held) on a controlled programme.

| Technique | Property measured | Plot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) | Mass | Mass (%) vs temperature |
| Differential thermal analysis (DTA) | Temperature difference between sample and reference | ΔT vs temperature |
| Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) | Heat flow difference between sample and reference | Heat flow (mW) vs temperature |

Events seen on heating:

| Event | Mass change (TGA) | Heat (DTA/DSC) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loss of water or solvent (desolvation) | Loss | Endothermic |
| Melting | None | Endothermic, sharp |
| Boiling, sublimation | Loss | Endothermic |
| Crystallisation of an amorphous solid | None | Exothermic |
| Glass transition | None | Step in baseline (change in heat capacity), not a peak |
| Polymorphic transition | None | Endo or exo |
| Decomposition | Loss | Endo or exo |
| Oxidation in air | Gain (sometimes) then loss | Exothermic |

## 2.2 Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)

**Principle.** The sample is heated at a controlled rate in a chosen atmosphere and its **mass is recorded continuously**. A loss of mass at a particular temperature shows that a volatile part (water, solvent, CO2) has left or that the substance has decomposed. Mass changes give quantitative information directly.

**Thermogram.** A TGA curve is a series of plateaus (stable compounds) and steps (mass losses). The first derivative, **DTG** (dm/dt vs T), turns each step into a peak; the peak top is the temperature of fastest loss and helps separate overlapping steps.

**Instrumentation**

```text
          Recording / computer  <── balance control unit
                    ^                     |
                    |               Thermobalance (null-point microbalance)
                    |                     | hang-down wire
    Temperature programmer ──> Furnace [ sample pan  + thermocouple ]  <── purge gas (N2, air)
```

| Part | Details |
| --- | --- |
| **Thermobalance** | Sensitive microbalance (microgram resolution), usually **null-point** type: when the pan moves, an electromagnetic force restores it, and the restoring current is proportional to the mass change. Kept outside the hot zone |
| **Sample holder (crucible)** | Platinum, alumina or quartz pan, a few mg of sample |
| **Furnace** | Electrically heated, up to about 1000–1500 °C; low thermal mass for fast, uniform heating |
| **Temperature programmer and sensor** | Thermocouple close to the sample; linear heating rate, often 5–20 °C/min |
| **Purge gas** | Nitrogen or argon (inert) or air/oxygen (oxidising); also carries away volatile products |
| **Recorder / data system** | Plots mass against temperature and computes DTG |

**Factors affecting the TGA curve**

1. **Heating rate:** faster heating shifts losses to higher temperatures and can merge steps.
2. **Sample mass and particle size:** large or coarse samples heat unevenly and release gas slowly.
3. **Atmosphere:** inert vs oxidising gas changes the reactions; flow rate matters.
4. **Crucible shape and material:** a deep crucible traps vapour; some metals catalyse reactions.
5. **Buoyancy:** the gas around the pan gets less dense on heating, giving an apparent mass gain that must be corrected by a blank run.
6. **Packing of the sample** and condensation of volatiles on the cooler parts of the balance.

**Worked example 1: calcium oxalate monohydrate**, CaC2O4·H2O (Mr about 146.1), a standard test material, loses mass in three steps:

| Step | Reaction | Mass lost | Residue left |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (about 100–200 °C) | CaC2O4·H2O → CaC2O4 + H2O | 18.0 g/mol → 12.3% | 87.7% |
| 2 (about 400–500 °C) | CaC2O4 → CaCO3 + CO | 28.0 g/mol → 19.2% | 68.5% |
| 3 (about 650–850 °C) | CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 | 44.0 g/mol → 30.1% | 38.4% (CaO) |

Each percentage = (mass of lost molecule / 146.1) × 100. A good match between measured and calculated losses confirms the instrument is working and the composition is right.

**Worked example 2: is a theophylline sample the monohydrate?** Anhydrous theophylline C7H8N4O2 has Mr about 180.2; the monohydrate about 198.2. Expected water loss = 18.0/198.2 × 100 = **9.1%**. A loss of about 9% below about 120 °C fits the monohydrate; much less suggests partial dehydration.

**Applications of TGA in pharmacy**

1. Water and solvent content of drugs and excipients; distinguishing **hydrates and solvates** from adsorbed surface moisture.
2. Thermal stability and decomposition temperature; temperature limits for drying and processing.
3. Composition of mixtures and of inorganic residues (ash, filler content).
4. Kinetics of decomposition (activation energy) for stability prediction.
5. Evaluating packaging polymers and excipients (cellulose derivatives, starch).
6. Combined with DSC or with an IR or mass spectrometer to identify the gas released (evolved gas analysis).

## 2.3 Differential thermal analysis (DTA)

**Principle.** The sample and an **inert reference** (calcined alumina) are heated side by side in the same furnace at the same rate. A thermocouple in each measures temperature, and the **difference ΔT = T(sample) − T(reference)** is recorded against the reference (or furnace) temperature. When nothing happens, ΔT is zero (baseline). An endothermic change makes the sample lag behind (ΔT negative, downward peak by convention); an exothermic change makes it run ahead (upward peak).

```text
    ΔT
     ^                         exothermic (crystallisation, oxidation)
     |                 /\
  0  |______    _____/  \________
     |      \  /
     |       \/   endothermic (melting, dehydration)
     +-----------------------------------> Temperature
```

**Instrumentation**

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Furnace with temperature programmer | Heats both cups at a linear rate |
| Sample and reference holders | Twin cups in a metal or ceramic block, placed symmetrically |
| Differential thermocouple | Two junctions connected in opposition so the output is proportional to ΔT |
| Second thermocouple | Measures the sample or block temperature |
| Atmosphere control | Inert or reactive gas |
| Amplifier and recorder | ΔT is small, so it is amplified and plotted |

**Factors affecting DTA:** heating rate, sample mass and packing, particle size, thermal conductivity of sample vs reference, thermocouple position, atmosphere, and the dilution of the sample with reference material.

**Applications:** melting point and purity checks, polymorphic transitions, dehydration, decomposition, identification by comparing thermograms, phase diagrams and drug–excipient interactions. Peak area is proportional to the heat change, but DTA is mostly **qualitative**, because the relation between area and enthalpy depends on the instrument and sample.

## 2.4 Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)

**Principle.** DSC measures the **difference in heat flow** (energy per unit time, mW) needed to keep the sample and an empty reference pan on the same temperature programme. Peak area gives the enthalpy change directly, so DSC is **quantitative**.

**Two types**

| Feature | Power-compensation DSC | Heat-flux DSC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heaters | Separate heater and sensor for sample and reference | One furnace heats both |
| What is measured | Extra electrical power fed to keep both at the same temperature | Temperature difference across a disc of known thermal resistance, converted to heat flow |
| Response | Very fast | Robust, good baseline |
| Relation to DTA | — | A calibrated, quantitative form of DTA |

```text
 Power-compensation DSC
   [sample pan] heater S + sensor S        [reference pan] heater R + sensor R
          \                                       /
           +-------> controller keeps T(S) = T(R) <-+
                         |
                 ΔP = dH/dt  ──> recorder: heat flow vs temperature
```

**The DSC curve.** Endothermic peaks (melting) are drawn downward or upward depending on the instrument's convention, so always read the label "endo ↓" or "exo ↑". From one curve you read:

- **Onset temperature** (extrapolated start) — taken as the melting point of a pure substance.
- **Peak temperature.**
- **Peak area** → enthalpy of fusion ΔHf (J/g).
- **Glass transition (Tg):** a step in the baseline of amorphous materials.
- **Cold crystallisation:** an exotherm as amorphous material crystallises on heating.

**Calibration.** Temperature and enthalpy are calibrated with high-purity metals of known melting point and heat of fusion, most often **indium** (mp 156.6 °C, ΔHf about 28.5 J/g); zinc and tin cover other ranges. Heat capacity is calibrated with sapphire.

**Purity by DSC.** Impurities lower and broaden the melting peak. For eutectic impurities, the **van't Hoff equation** relates the sample temperature Ts to the fraction melted F:

**Ts = T0 − (R T0² x2 / ΔHf) × (1/F)**

where T0 is the melting point of pure substance and x2 the mole fraction of impurity. Plotting Ts against 1/F gives a straight line whose slope gives x2. This works for fairly pure (above about 98 mol%) substances that melt without decomposing.

**Factors affecting DSC:** heating rate, sample mass, pan type (open, crimped, hermetic, pin-holed), purge gas, particle size and contact with the pan, and thermal history of the sample.

**Pharmaceutical applications of DSC**

1. **Polymorphism:** different polymorphs show different melting points and enthalpies; transitions between forms appear as extra peaks.
2. **Purity determination** (van't Hoff).
3. **Drug–excipient compatibility** in preformulation: a peak that shifts or disappears in a physical mixture warns of interaction.
4. **Glass transition** of amorphous drugs, solid dispersions and polymers; stability of amorphous forms.
5. **Hydrates and solvates** (with TGA).
6. **Lyophilisation:** finding the collapse or eutectic temperature to design freeze-drying cycles.
7. **Liposomes and lipid excipients:** phase transition temperature of phospholipids.
8. **Protein stability:** unfolding (denaturation) temperature.

**DTA vs DSC**

| Point | DTA | DSC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measures | ΔT between sample and reference | Difference in heat flow (energy) |
| Output | °C vs T | mW vs T |
| Quantitative enthalpy | Approximate | Accurate |
| Temperature range | Can go very high (above 1000 °C) | Usually to about 700 °C |
| Main use | Qualitative transitions, high-temperature inorganic work | Quantitative pharmaceutical solid-state work |

## 2.5 Origin of X-rays

**X-rays** are electromagnetic radiation of very short wavelength, about 0.01–10 nm (0.1–100 Å). Wavelengths near 1 Å match the spacing between atoms in crystals, which is why crystals diffract them.

**X-ray tube (Coolidge tube).** A heated tungsten filament (cathode) emits electrons. A high voltage (about 30–50 kV) accelerates them onto a metal target (anode: copper, molybdenum, cobalt, chromium) in an evacuated tube. Only about 1% of the energy becomes X-rays; the rest is heat, so the anode is water-cooled. X-rays leave through beryllium windows.

```text
   filament (−) e⁻ e⁻ e⁻ ───────────>  target anode (+, water-cooled Cu)
   (heated W)        high voltage            │
                                             └──> X-rays out through Be window
```

Two kinds of X-rays are produced:

1. **Continuous (white) radiation, bremsstrahlung:** electrons slow down in the field of the target nuclei and give a smooth range of wavelengths. The shortest wavelength depends only on the voltage: λmin = hc/eV. At 30 kV, λmin ≈ 0.41 Å; at 40 kV, about 0.31 Å (Duane–Hunt law).
2. **Characteristic (line) radiation:** an incoming electron knocks out an inner (K-shell) electron of a target atom. An electron from the L or M shell drops into the hole and emits an X-ray of a fixed energy, characteristic of the target metal: **Kα** (L → K) and **Kβ** (M → K). Copper Kα is about 1.54 Å; molybdenum Kα about 0.71 Å.

**Moseley's law:** the square root of the frequency of a characteristic line is proportional to the atomic number (√ν ∝ Z − σ). This founded X-ray fluorescence analysis of elements.

**Monochromatic X-rays** are needed for diffraction. A **filter** removes Kβ: a nickel foil absorbs Cu Kβ much more than Cu Kα (its absorption edge lies between them). A crystal monochromator (graphite) is also used.

**Detectors:** photographic film (older cameras), Geiger–Müller and proportional counters, scintillation counters, and modern solid-state and area detectors (CCD, pixel detectors).

## 2.6 Basic aspects of crystals

A **crystal** is a solid whose atoms or molecules repeat in a regular three-dimensional pattern. An **amorphous** solid (glass) has no long-range order.

- **Lattice:** the array of points that repeats the pattern.
- **Unit cell:** the smallest repeating box, defined by edge lengths a, b, c and angles α, β, γ.
- **Seven crystal systems** and **fourteen Bravais lattices.**

| Crystal system | Edges | Angles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cubic | a = b = c | α = β = γ = 90° |
| Tetragonal | a = b ≠ c | all 90° |
| Orthorhombic | a ≠ b ≠ c | all 90° |
| Monoclinic | a ≠ b ≠ c | α = γ = 90°, β ≠ 90° |
| Triclinic | a ≠ b ≠ c | α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90° |
| Hexagonal | a = b ≠ c | α = β = 90°, γ = 120° |
| Rhombohedral (trigonal) | a = b = c | α = β = γ ≠ 90° |

Most organic drugs crystallise in the low-symmetry monoclinic, triclinic or orthorhombic systems.

**Miller indices (h k l)** name a family of parallel lattice planes: take the intercepts of a plane on the a, b and c axes in unit-cell lengths, take reciprocals and clear fractions. For a cubic cell the spacing between (h k l) planes is

**d = a / √(h² + k² + l²)**

**Polymorphism:** the ability of one compound to crystallise in more than one arrangement. Polymorphs differ in melting point, solubility, dissolution rate, stability and sometimes bioavailability. **Pseudopolymorphs** are hydrates and solvates.

## 2.7 Bragg's law

X-rays scattered by electrons in successive parallel planes reinforce each other only when the extra path travelled by the lower ray is a whole number of wavelengths.

```text
 incident        reflected
     \   θ   θ   /
  ----\-----.---/-------  plane 1
       \    |  /            extra path = 2d sinθ
  ------\---.-/---------  plane 2       (d = spacing between planes)
 Constructive interference when 2d sinθ = nλ
```

**nλ = 2d sinθ**

where n is the order (usually 1), λ the wavelength, d the interplanar spacing and θ the glancing (Bragg) angle. Diffractometers record the angle **2θ** between the incident and diffracted beams.

**Worked examples (Cu Kα, λ = 1.5406 Å, n = 1)**

| Observed 2θ | θ | d = λ/(2 sinθ) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10° | 5° | 8.84 Å |
| 20° | 10° | 4.44 Å |
| 30° | 15° | 2.98 Å |

Sodium chloride is cubic with a = 5.64 Å. For the (200) planes, d = 5.64/√4 = 2.82 Å, so sinθ = 1.5406/(2 × 2.82) = 0.273, θ ≈ 15.9° and the peak appears at **2θ ≈ 31.7°**. For the (111) planes, d = 5.64/√3 = 3.26 Å, giving 2θ ≈ 27.4°.

## 2.8 X-ray crystallography and diffraction methods

| Method | Radiation | Sample | Movement | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Laue method** | Polychromatic (white) | Single crystal | Stationary | Spot pattern showing symmetry and orientation of the crystal |
| **Rotating crystal method** | Monochromatic | Single crystal | Crystal rotated about one axis | Layer lines of spots on a cylindrical film; unit-cell dimensions |
| **Single crystal diffractometry** | Monochromatic | Single crystal (about 0.1–0.5 mm) | Rotated through many orientations (goniometer) | Intensities of thousands of reflections → complete 3D structure |
| **Powder method** (Debye–Scherrer; powder diffractometer) | Monochromatic | Fine powder, random orientation | Sample or detector scanned through 2θ | Rings or a diffractogram of peaks at characteristic 2θ: the fingerprint of a crystal form |

### Rotating crystal technique

A single crystal is mounted so that one of its axes is perpendicular to a monochromatic beam and is rotated (or oscillated) about that axis. A cylindrical film surrounds the crystal. As the crystal turns, each set of planes passes through its Bragg angle and gives a spot. The spots lie on horizontal **layer lines**; their spacing gives the repeat distance along the rotation axis, and their positions are used to index reflections and find the unit cell. Oscillating or Weissenberg variations reduce overlap of spots.

### Single crystal diffraction

```text
 X-ray tube ─> monochromator ─> collimator ─> crystal on goniometer head ─> area detector
                                                (rotated in 3 axes; often cooled to about 100 K)
                                  computer: indexing, intensities, structure solution, refinement
```

1. A good single crystal is mounted on a goniometer and rotated through many orientations.
2. Positions of the spots give the unit cell and crystal system; systematic absences give the space group.
3. Intensities of the spots depend on where the atoms are. Each intensity gives the amplitude of a structure factor, but the phase is lost (**the phase problem**).
4. Phases are estimated by direct methods (small molecules) or Patterson and heavy-atom methods; a Fourier synthesis then gives an **electron-density map**.
5. Atoms are placed in the density peaks and the model is refined until calculated and observed intensities agree (low R-factor).
6. Output: exact bond lengths, bond angles, conformation, absolute configuration (stereochemistry) and hydrogen-bonding packing.

### Powder diffraction (PXRD)

A finely powdered sample contains crystallites in every orientation, so for every set of planes some crystallites are always at the Bragg angle. In a **powder diffractometer** (Bragg–Brentano geometry) the sample sits flat on a holder; as the tube and detector move, the detector counts intensity against 2θ.

- **Peak positions (2θ → d)** identify the crystal form.
- **Relative peak intensities** confirm the identity (they can be distorted by preferred orientation of needle or plate crystals).
- **Peak width** relates to crystallite size; the **Scherrer equation** τ = Kλ/(β cosθ) estimates size from the extra breadth β (in radians). Example: K = 0.9, λ = 1.5406 Å, β = 0.20°, 2θ = 20° → τ ≈ 40 nm.
- **Amorphous material** gives a broad hump ("halo") with no sharp peaks.

## 2.9 Structural elucidation and applications of XRD

1. **Complete three-dimensional structure** of drugs, natural products and proteins (single crystal); absolute configuration of chiral drugs. Drug–receptor and enzyme complexes are solved this way for structure-based drug design.
2. **Identification of polymorphs and pseudopolymorphs** (PXRD fingerprint); controlling the right form in API and tablets.
3. **Degree of crystallinity** and detection of amorphous content, for example after milling or in solid dispersions.
4. **Quantitative phase analysis:** amount of an unwanted polymorph in a mixture from peak intensities.
5. **Monitoring form changes** during granulation, drying, compression and storage (stability).
6. **Identification of unknown crystalline substances** by comparing d-spacings with reference patterns.
7. **Crystallite size and strain** (Scherrer).
8. **Protecting patents:** a new crystal form is often defined by its PXRD peaks.
9. **Excipients:** crystallinity of lactose, cellulose and other excipients.

## Remember

- TGA = mass vs T (null-point thermobalance); DTG separates steps; calcium oxalate monohydrate loses 12.3%, 19.2%, 30.1%.
- DTA = ΔT vs T (qualitative); DSC = heat flow vs T (quantitative ΔH); indium calibrates DSC.
- Endothermic: melting, dehydration; exothermic: crystallisation, oxidation; Tg is a baseline step.
- DSC purity: van't Hoff, Ts vs 1/F.
- X-rays: bremsstrahlung (λmin = hc/eV) + characteristic Kα, Kβ; Ni filter removes Cu Kβ; Cu Kα about 1.54 Å.
- Seven crystal systems, fourteen Bravais lattices; cubic d = a/√(h² + k² + l²).
- Bragg: nλ = 2d sinθ; diffractometers read 2θ.
- Laue (white, stationary), rotating crystal (monochromatic, rotated), single crystal (full structure), powder (fingerprint of polymorphs).
