# Unit 3: Calibration and validation of instruments

A result is only as trustworthy as the instrument that produced it. A balance that reads 0.5% high or a spectrophotometer whose wavelength has drifted by 3 nm will pass or fail batches wrongly, and regulators treat that as a serious GMP failure. This unit explains the vocabulary (calibration, qualification, validation), the ICH and US FDA expectations, the parameters used to validate an analytical method, and how each common laboratory instrument is calibrated.

## 3.1 Key terms

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Calibration** | Comparing an instrument's readings with a traceable standard of known value over its working range, and adjusting or recording the error | Checking a balance with certified weights; checking UV wavelength with holmium |
| **Qualification** | Documented proof that equipment is correctly designed, installed, operates and performs as intended | DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ of a new HPLC |
| **Validation** | Documented evidence giving a high degree of assurance that a process, method or system consistently produces a result meeting its predetermined specifications | Validating an HPLC assay method; validating a granulation process |
| **Verification** | Confirming that an already validated (for example pharmacopoeial) method works in your laboratory | Running accuracy and precision on an IP method |
| **Traceability** | An unbroken chain of comparisons linking a measurement to national or international standards | Weights certified against national standards |
| **System suitability test (SST)** | A check, run with each analysis, that the whole system (instrument + column + method) is working on that day | Resolution, tailing, RSD of replicate injections |

**Calibration vs validation.** Calibration checks **one instrument's accuracy** against standards; validation shows that a **process or method** is fit for purpose. An instrument must be qualified and calibrated before any method on it can be validated.

## 3.2 Regulatory basis

- **ICH guidelines** (International Council for Harmonisation):
  - **Q2(R1) "Validation of Analytical Procedures: Text and Methodology"**, now revised as **Q2(R2)**, together with **Q14** on analytical procedure development. These define the validation characteristics used worldwide.
  - **Q7** (GMP for active pharmaceutical ingredients) requires calibrated equipment and validated processes.
  - Q8 (pharmaceutical development), Q9 (quality risk management) and Q10 (pharmaceutical quality system) support a risk-based, lifecycle approach.
- **US FDA:**
  - **21 CFR Part 211** (cGMP for finished pharmaceuticals): equipment must be routinely calibrated, inspected or checked according to a written programme (§211.68), and laboratory controls must include calibration of instruments at suitable intervals with specifications, limits and remedial action (§211.160).
  - **Guidance for Industry: Process Validation — General Principles and Practices (2011):** a lifecycle with three stages: **Stage 1 process design, Stage 2 process qualification, Stage 3 continued process verification.**
  - **Guidance on Analytical Procedures and Methods Validation** (2015).
  - **21 CFR Part 11:** electronic records and signatures for computerised instruments (audit trail, access control).
- **USP general chapter <1058> Analytical Instrument Qualification** describes the 4Q model and classifies instruments by complexity.
- In India, **Schedule M** of the Drugs Rules requires calibrated equipment and validated processes, following WHO GMP.

## 3.3 Qualification of equipment (the 4Q model)

```text
  DQ ────────> IQ ────────> OQ ────────> PQ ────────> routine use with
 (right design) (installed    (works over   (works for the   calibration, maintenance,
                 correctly)    its ranges)   real method)    requalification after change
```

| Stage | Question answered | Typical checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Design qualification (DQ)** | Is this the right instrument for our needs? | User requirement specification (URS), vendor selection, specifications match intended use |
| **Installation qualification (IQ)** | Has it been delivered and installed correctly? | Components against purchase order, site (power, gas, environment), software version, manuals, connections, serial numbers |
| **Operational qualification (OQ)** | Does it work as specified over its operating range? | Wavelength accuracy, flow-rate accuracy, temperature accuracy, detector linearity, alarms |
| **Performance qualification (PQ)** | Does it consistently perform for the intended analysis? | Running real or standard samples under routine conditions; system suitability over time |

Requalification is done after major repair, relocation or software upgrade, and periodically as per SOP.

## 3.4 Validation: types and lifecycle

**Process validation types (traditional classification)**

| Type | When done | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prospective** | Before the product is sold; usually on consecutive validation batches | Preferred for new products |
| **Concurrent** | During routine production, batches released as they are validated | Used in special cases (limited batches, urgent need) |
| **Retrospective** | Using historical data of batches already made | No longer generally accepted for new products |
| **Revalidation** | After changes in formula, equipment, site or process, or periodically | Triggered by change control |

**Validation master plan (VMP):** the top document listing what will be validated, by whom, how and when. Each validation has a **protocol** (approved before work starts, with acceptance criteria) and a **report** (results, deviations, conclusion).

## 3.5 Analytical method validation (ICH Q2)

**Validation characteristics**

| Characteristic | Definition | How it is usually shown |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Specificity** | Ability to measure the analyte unequivocally in the presence of impurities, degradants and matrix | Placebo and spiked samples; forced degradation (acid, base, oxidation, heat, light); peak purity with a PDA detector; resolution from nearest peak |
| **Accuracy** | Closeness of the result to the true value | % recovery of known amounts spiked into placebo; at least 9 determinations over 3 levels (for example 80, 100, 120%, 3 replicates each) |
| **Precision** | Closeness of agreement among repeated results (expressed as SD or RSD) | See the three levels below |
| – Repeatability | Same analyst, same day, same instrument | At least 9 determinations over the range, or 6 at 100% |
| – Intermediate precision | Within one laboratory: different days, analysts, instruments | Compare RSD across the variations |
| – Reproducibility | Between laboratories | Collaborative studies; for standardising methods |
| **Detection limit (LOD)** | Lowest amount that can be detected, not necessarily quantified | Signal-to-noise about 3 : 1, or 3.3σ/S |
| **Quantitation limit (LOQ)** | Lowest amount that can be measured with acceptable accuracy and precision | Signal-to-noise about 10 : 1, or 10σ/S |
| **Linearity** | Results directly proportional to concentration within a range | At least 5 concentrations; regression line, correlation coefficient, slope, intercept, residuals |
| **Range** | Interval between upper and lower concentration with suitable accuracy, precision and linearity | Assay: usually 80–120% of test concentration; content uniformity 70–130%; dissolution ±20% over the specified range; impurities from reporting level to 120% of the limit |
| **Robustness** | Capacity to stay unaffected by small deliberate changes | Vary pH, mobile-phase ratio, flow rate, column temperature, column lot, wavelength |

In LOD and LOQ, σ is the standard deviation of the response (of the blank or of the y-intercept) and S is the slope of the calibration line.

**Which characteristics are needed?**

| Characteristic | Identification | Impurity: quantitative | Impurity: limit test | Assay (content, dissolution) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | − | + | − | + |
| Repeatability | − | + | − | + |
| Intermediate precision | − | + | − | + |
| Specificity | + | + | + | + |
| Detection limit | − | − (may be needed) | + | − |
| Quantitation limit | − | + | − | − |
| Linearity | − | + | − | + |
| Range | − | + | − | + |

**Worked example 1: LOD and LOQ.** A UV calibration line has slope S = 0.052 absorbance per µg/ml, and the standard deviation of the blank response is σ = 0.0021.
LOD = 3.3 × 0.0021/0.052 = **0.13 µg/ml**; LOQ = 10 × 0.0021/0.052 = **0.40 µg/ml**.

**Worked example 2: accuracy.** Placebo spiked with 10.00 mg of drug; found 9.87 mg. Recovery = 9.87/10.00 × 100 = **98.7%**.

**Worked example 3: repeatability.** Six assays at 100% give 99.6, 100.4, 99.1, 100.8, 100.2 and 99.5% of label claim. Mean = 99.93%; SD = 0.64; **RSD = SD/mean × 100 = 0.64%**, well within a typical limit of 2% for an assay.

**System suitability (chromatographic methods).** Before each run, a standard is injected and typical checks are made: resolution between the critical pair (baseline separation needs Rs of at least 1.5; many methods ask for 2), tailing factor (commonly not more than 2), theoretical plates (N), and RSD of replicate standard injections (commonly not more than 2% for 5–6 injections). Exact limits are written in each monograph or method.

## 3.6 General calibration programme

1. A **master list** of instruments, each with a unique ID and calibration frequency.
2. **Written SOP** for each instrument: standards, procedure, acceptance limits, frequency (daily check, monthly, six-monthly, after repair).
3. **Certified reference standards** traceable to national standards.
4. **Records:** date, standards used, readings, pass/fail, signature, next due date.
5. **Status label** on the instrument ("Calibrated on … Due on …"; "Under maintenance; do not use").
6. **Out-of-calibration action:** remove from use, investigate the impact on results since the last good calibration, repair, recalibrate, and record the deviation.

## 3.7 Calibration of an electronic balance

**Before calibration:** place on a firm, vibration-free bench away from draughts and direct sunlight; check the level bubble; switch on and allow warm-up; clean the pan; use tweezers to handle weights; use certified weights of suitable accuracy class (for example OIML E2 or F1).

| Test | Procedure | What it detects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Daily check (sensitivity / accuracy)** | Weigh one or two certified weights (for example near the usual load) after internal or external adjustment | Drift in span |
| **Repeatability** | Weigh the same weight about 10 times, taring between readings; calculate SD | Random scatter |
| **Eccentricity (corner load)** | Place a weight in the centre, then at four corners of the pan; compare | Error when sample is off-centre |
| **Linearity** | Weigh certified weights across the range (for example 10%, 25%, 50%, 100% of capacity) | Non-proportional response |
| **Minimum weight** | From the repeatability SD | Smallest sample that can be weighed accurately |

**USP <41> criteria (used widely for analytical weighing):**
- Repeatability is satisfactory if 2 × SD / (smallest net weight intended) ≤ 0.10%. If the SD is below 0.41d (d = readability), 0.41d is used instead.
- Accuracy is satisfactory if the weight reading is within 0.10% of the test weight's value.

**Worked example: minimum weight.** A balance with readability d = 0.01 mg gives SD = 0.008 mg for 10 weighings. Because 0.008 is greater than 0.41 × 0.01 = 0.0041, use 0.008. Minimum weight = 2 × 0.008/0.001 = **16 mg**. Samples below 16 mg should not be weighed on this balance for assays.

## 3.8 Calibration of a UV-visible spectrophotometer

The Indian Pharmacopoeia and other pharmacopoeias prescribe these checks:

| Parameter | Standard | Procedure and acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Control of wavelength** | Holmium perchlorate solution (maxima at 241.15, 287.15, 361.5 and 536.3 nm), holmium oxide glass filter, mercury lamp lines, or the deuterium lamp lines at 486.0 and 656.1 nm | Scan and note peak positions. Permitted tolerance: ±1 nm in the ultraviolet and ±3 nm in the visible region |
| **Control of absorbance (photometric accuracy)** | Potassium dichromate dried to constant weight at 130 °C; about 57–63 mg dissolved in 0.005 M H2SO4 and diluted to 1000 ml | Measure absorbance at 235, 257, 313 and 350 nm and calculate A(1%, 1 cm). Nominal values: about 124.5, 144.5, 48.6 and 106.6 respectively, each within the narrow range given in the pharmacopoeia |
| **Limit of stray light** | Potassium chloride 1.2% w/v in water | Absorbance at about 200 nm (1 cm cell, water as blank) should be greater than 2.0 |
| **Resolution (spectral bandwidth)** | Toluene 0.02% v/v in hexane | Ratio of absorbance at the maximum near 269 nm to the minimum near 266 nm should be at least 1.5 |
| **Cells** | Fill matched cells with the same solvent | Absorbance difference within the tolerance in the SOP; clean, unscratched, quartz below about 350 nm |
| **Baseline flatness, noise, drift** | Air or solvent vs solvent | As per manufacturer and SOP |

**Why each test matters:** wrong wavelength puts you off the λmax, where absorbance changes steeply; wrong absorbance scale gives wrong assays directly; stray light makes high absorbances read too low (negative deviation from Beer's law); poor resolution flattens sharp bands.

## 3.9 Calibration of an IR spectrophotometer

| Parameter | Standard | Procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wavenumber accuracy** | Polystyrene film (about 35 µm thick) | Record the spectrum; check positions of reference bands such as 3060.0, 2849.5, 1942.9, 1601.2, 1583.0, 1154.5 and 1028.3 cm⁻¹ within the tolerances given in the pharmacopoeia (about ±1 to ±2 cm⁻¹) |
| **Resolution** | Polystyrene film | Depth of the trough between closely spaced bands (for example between 2870 and 2849.5 cm⁻¹, and between 1589 and 1583 cm⁻¹) in %T must exceed the stated values |
| **Transmittance (100% line), noise** | Empty beam | Flat line near 100% T; noise within limits |
| **Energy / throughput** | Single-beam energy at set wavenumbers (FTIR) | Compared with installation values to check source and detector ageing |

Keep the KBr, cells and instrument dry: water vapour and CO2 bands (near 3700, 1600 and 2350 cm⁻¹) are a common source of error. FTIR instruments also run an internal laser reference that keeps the wavenumber scale accurate.

## 3.10 Calibration of a fluorimeter

| Parameter | Standard | Procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wavelength accuracy** | Xenon or mercury lamp emission lines; Raman band of water | With excitation at 350 nm, the water Raman band appears near 397 nm (the O–H stretch of about 3400 cm⁻¹ subtracted from the excitation wavenumber: 28,571 − 3400 = 25,171 cm⁻¹ → about 397 nm). Its position checks the emission scale |
| **Sensitivity (signal-to-noise)** | Water Raman band | Ratio of the Raman peak to the noise must exceed the manufacturer's value |
| **Linearity of response** | **Quinine sulfate** in 0.05 M (0.1 N) H2SO4 at several concentrations; excitation about 350 nm, emission about 450 nm | Plot fluorescence vs concentration; check the correlation coefficient; check the low-concentration range, since self-absorption bends the line at high concentration |
| **Stability** | Standard solution read over time | Drift within limits |
| **Blank** | Solvent and cell | Low, constant background; clean, fluorescence-free cells |

Halides quench quinine fluorescence, so the dilutions must be made in sulfuric acid, not hydrochloric acid.

## 3.11 Calibration of a flame photometer

1. Check gas supply, air pressure and flame steadiness; let the burner warm up.
2. Check the filters: sodium at 589 nm, potassium at 766 nm (lithium at 671 nm if used).
3. Aspirate distilled water and set zero; aspirate the top standard and set full scale.
4. **Linearity:** aspirate a series of standard solutions of NaCl or KCl (for example 10–100 ppm of the metal) and plot emission vs concentration; the working range must be linear (self-absorption bends the curve at high concentration).
5. **Repeatability:** aspirate one standard several times; RSD within the SOP limit.
6. **Interference check:** measure sodium in the presence of potassium and vice versa; mutual excitation and ionisation can raise or lower readings.
7. **Response time and drift:** re-check zero and the top standard after every few samples and at the end.

## 3.12 Calibration of HPLC

Each module is calibrated separately and then the system as a whole.

| Module | Parameter | Typical method (limits as per SOP or manufacturer) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pump** | Flow-rate accuracy | Pump water or methanol at set flows (for example 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 ml/min); collect into a volumetric flask and time it, or weigh the eluate; measured flow commonly within ±2% of set value |
| | Flow precision | RSD of retention times of repeated injections |
| | Gradient composition accuracy | Channel A water, channel B water containing a UV tracer (acetone or caffeine); run step gradients (for example 10, 50, 90% B) and compare step heights with expected values |
| | Pressure test | Block the outlet and check pressure holding (leak test) |
| **Injector / autosampler** | Precision | 6 injections of a standard; RSD of peak area (commonly not more than 1%) |
| | Linearity of injection volume | Inject different volumes; area vs volume should be linear |
| | Carry-over | Inject blank after a concentrated standard; peak in blank below a set % |
| **Detector (UV/PDA)** | Wavelength accuracy | Caffeine solution (maxima near 205 and 273 nm) or built-in holmium filter |
| | Linearity | Caffeine solutions over the range; correlation coefficient close to 1 |
| | Noise and drift | Mobile phase flowing, no injection, over a fixed time |
| **Column oven** | Temperature accuracy | Calibrated thermometer or probe at set temperatures; commonly within ±2 °C |
| **Whole system** | System suitability | Plates, tailing, resolution, RSD with a test mixture |

## 3.13 Calibration of GC

| Part | Parameter | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Carrier gas** | Flow-rate accuracy | Bubble flowmeter or digital flowmeter at the column or detector outlet; compare with set flow |
| **Oven** | Temperature accuracy and stability | Calibrated probe at several set temperatures; check isothermal stability and programmed ramp rate |
| **Injector** | Temperature; split ratio; injection precision | Probe; replicate injections of a standard (for example a mixture of n-alkanes or a solvent mixture); RSD of area and retention time |
| **Detector (FID)** | Sensitivity and linearity | Inject a series of concentrations of a test compound; check detector response, noise and linear range; check hydrogen and air flows |
| **Whole system** | Retention time reproducibility, resolution | Test mixture with known peaks |

Leak checks of the gas lines and septum and replacement of the septum and liner are part of routine GC maintenance.

## Remember

- Calibration = instrument vs traceable standard; qualification = DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ; validation = documented evidence a method or process works consistently.
- ICH Q2(R1)/Q2(R2) parameters: specificity, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate, reproducibility), LOD, LOQ, linearity, range, robustness.
- LOD = 3.3σ/S; LOQ = 10σ/S; assay range 80–120%; at least 5 levels for linearity, 9 determinations for accuracy.
- US FDA: 21 CFR 211.68 and 211.160; 2011 process validation = design, qualification, continued verification.
- Balance: repeatability, eccentricity, linearity; USP <41>: 2 × SD/weight ≤ 0.10%; minimum weight = 2000 × SD.
- UV: holmium (wavelength), potassium dichromate (absorbance), KCl (stray light), toluene in hexane (resolution, ratio ≥ 1.5).
- IR: polystyrene film; fluorimeter: quinine sulfate and water Raman band; flame: NaCl and KCl standards.
- HPLC: flow rate, gradient, injector precision, detector wavelength and linearity, oven temperature; GC: gas flow, oven temperature, injector, FID linearity.

# Unit 4: Radioimmunoassay and extraction techniques

Hormones, many drugs and tumour markers circulate in blood at nanogram or even picogram per millilitre levels, mixed with thousands of other substances. Measuring them needs two things: a method sensitive and specific enough to find a tiny amount (radioimmunoassay was the first to do this), and a way to pull the analyte out of the sample before analysis (solid-phase and liquid–liquid extraction). This unit covers both.

## 4.1 Radioimmunoassay: importance

**Radioimmunoassay (RIA)** is an analytical method that measures a substance (antigen) by its **competition with a radioactively labelled form of the same substance for a limited number of binding sites on a specific antibody**.

It was developed by **Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson** around 1959–1960 to measure insulin in human plasma. Yalow received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1977 for this work.

**Why it mattered**

1. **Very high sensitivity:** picogram to nanogram amounts, far below what UV or HPLC with UV detection could measure in plasma.
2. **High specificity** from the antibody–antigen reaction.
3. Works directly in small volumes of serum or plasma, often without extraction.
4. Can handle large numbers of samples.
5. It started the whole family of immunoassays (ELISA, chemiluminescence, fluorescence immunoassays) that now dominate clinical laboratories.

## 4.2 Components of RIA

| Component | Role | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Antigen (analyte)** | The substance to be measured, in standards and samples | Hormone, drug, protein |
| **Labelled antigen (tracer)** | Same antigen carrying a radioisotope; competes with the unlabelled antigen | Must keep its ability to bind the antibody; high specific activity needed |
| **Specific antibody (antiserum)** | Binds the antigen; used in a **limited** amount so not all antigen can be bound | Raised in animals; small molecules (haptens) are first coupled to a carrier protein to make them immunogenic. Judged by **titre, affinity and specificity (low cross-reactivity)** |
| **Standards** | Known concentrations of pure antigen to build the standard curve | Prepared in the same matrix as samples |
| **Separation system** | Separates antibody-bound from free antigen | See section 4.5 |
| **Buffer and reagents** | Keep pH, ionic strength and protein content constant; prevent non-specific binding | Often contain albumin or gelatin |
| **Radioactivity counter** | Measures radioactivity of the bound (or free) fraction | **Gamma counter** for ¹²⁵I; **liquid scintillation counter** for ³H and ¹⁴C |

**Common isotopes**

| Isotope | Radiation | Half-life (approximate) | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ¹²⁵I | Gamma (and X-rays) | about 60 days | Most used; easy counting without sample preparation; high specific activity |
| ³H (tritium) | Weak beta | about 12.3 years | Little change to the molecule; needs liquid scintillation counting |
| ¹⁴C | Weak beta | about 5730 years | Low specific activity, so less used |

**Iodination methods** attach ¹²⁵I to tyrosine or histidine residues: **chloramine-T** (oxidising agent), **lactoperoxidase** (enzymatic, gentler) and **Bolton–Hunter reagent** (for molecules without tyrosine). After labelling, the tracer is purified from free iodide by gel filtration.

## 4.3 Principle of RIA

The method rests on the **law of mass action** and **competitive binding**:

```text
   Ag*   +   Ab   ⇌   Ag*–Ab     (labelled antigen, bound)
    +
   Ag                ⇌   Ag–Ab   (unlabelled antigen from sample or standard, bound)

   Fixed amounts: Ag* and Ab (Ab limited)
   Variable: Ag (unknown)
   More Ag in the sample  →  fewer sites left for Ag*  →  less radioactivity in the bound fraction
```

1. A fixed, limiting amount of antibody and a fixed amount of tracer are added to each tube.
2. Standards or samples (unlabelled antigen) are added.
3. Labelled and unlabelled antigen compete for the antibody sites; the system is incubated to equilibrium.
4. Bound (B) and free (F) antigen are separated.
5. The radioactivity of the bound fraction is counted.
6. **The bound radioactivity is inversely related to the concentration of antigen in the sample.**

**Standard (dose–response) curve.** Bound radioactivity is expressed as:

- **%B/T** — bound counts as a percentage of total counts added.
- **B/B0 (%)** — bound counts in a tube divided by bound counts in the zero-standard tube (no unlabelled antigen), × 100.

Plotting B/B0 against log concentration gives a falling **sigmoid curve**. A **logit–log plot**, logit(B/B0) = ln[(B/B0)/(1 − B/B0)] against log concentration, straightens it for easier reading. Unknowns are read from the curve.

```text
 B/B0 (%)
 100 |*****
     |      **
  50 |        ***      <- read unknown here
     |           **
   0 |             *******
     +---------------------------> log [antigen]
```

**Worked example.** Total counts added = 20,000 cpm. Zero standard (B0) binds 8000 cpm, so B0/T = 40%. A patient sample binds 4000 cpm. B/B0 = 4000/8000 × 100 = **50%**. The concentration is read from the standard curve at 50%; this mid-point region is the most precise part of the curve.

**Controls in each assay:** total count tubes, non-specific binding (NSB) tubes (no antibody), zero standard (B0), standards, quality-control samples, and unknowns, all in duplicate.

## 4.4 Steps of a typical RIA

1. Prepare standards over the expected range in drug-free serum.
2. Pipette buffer, standards, controls and samples into labelled tubes (duplicates).
3. Add a fixed volume of tracer to every tube.
4. Add a fixed volume of antibody (except total count and NSB tubes).
5. Mix and incubate (hours to overnight, at 4 °C or room temperature) to reach equilibrium.
6. Add the separation reagent; centrifuge; remove (decant or aspirate) the supernatant.
7. Count the radioactivity of the pellet (bound fraction) in a gamma counter.
8. Calculate B/B0, draw the standard curve and read the unknowns.

## 4.5 Methods of separating bound and free antigen

| Method | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **Adsorption** | Dextran-coated charcoal, talc or silicates adsorb the small free antigen; the large antibody–antigen complex stays in solution |
| **Precipitation with chemicals** | Ammonium sulfate, polyethylene glycol (PEG) or ethanol precipitate the antibody and its bound antigen |
| **Double antibody (second antibody) method** | A second antibody raised against the first antibody's species (for example anti-rabbit IgG made in goat) forms a precipitate with the first antibody and everything bound to it |
| **Solid-phase methods** | First antibody fixed to the tube wall, beads, or magnetic particles; free antigen simply washed away |
| **Chromatoelectrophoresis and gel filtration** | Early methods separating by charge or size |

## 4.6 Different methods (formats) of RIA

| Format | Principle | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Classical competitive (equilibrium) RIA** | Labelled and unlabelled antigen added together and compete | Standard format described above |
| **Sequential (disequilibrium, delayed addition) RIA** | Sample incubated with antibody first; tracer added later | Unlabelled antigen gets a head start, improving sensitivity |
| **Immunoradiometric assay (IRMA)** | The **antibody**, not the antigen, is labelled and used in excess; often a "sandwich" between a solid-phase antibody and a labelled second antibody | Non-competitive; signal **rises** with antigen concentration; wider range, better sensitivity; needs large antigens with two binding sites |
| **Solid-phase RIA** | Antibody-coated tubes or beads | Easy separation, suits automation |
| **Double antibody RIA** | Separation by second antibody | Very common in kits |

## 4.7 Limitations of RIA

1. **Radiation hazard** to staff; needs shielding, monitoring and licensing (in India from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board).
2. **Radioactive waste** needs special storage and disposal.
3. **Short shelf life** of ¹²⁵I tracers (about 60-day half-life) and radiolysis of labelled molecules.
4. **Expensive counters** and special laboratory facilities.
5. **Cross-reactivity:** metabolites or related substances may bind the antibody and give falsely high results.
6. Producing good antibodies takes time and animals.
7. Long incubation times; manual steps.
8. Measures immunoreactivity, which may not equal biological activity.

These limitations explain why many laboratories have moved to non-radioactive immunoassays (ELISA, chemiluminescence), but RIA remains a reference method for several hormones.

## 4.8 Applications of RIA

1. **Endocrinology:** insulin, growth hormone, thyroid hormones (T3, T4) and TSH, cortisol, oestradiol, progesterone, testosterone, LH, FSH, prolactin, hCG (pregnancy).
2. **Therapeutic drug monitoring:** digoxin and other drugs with a narrow therapeutic range.
3. **Pharmacokinetic and bioavailability studies** of drugs present at very low plasma levels.
4. **Drugs of abuse** screening (opiates and others) in forensic work.
5. **Tumour markers:** carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), prostate-specific antigen (PSA).
6. **Vitamins:** vitamin B12, folic acid.
7. **Infectious disease:** hepatitis B surface antigen and other viral antigens.
8. **Research:** neuropeptides, prostaglandins, cyclic nucleotides.

## 4.9 Extraction techniques: why extract?

Biological fluids, plant materials and formulations contain proteins, salts, lipids and excipients that interfere with analysis, clog columns, suppress MS signals and damage instruments. **Sample preparation** aims to:

- isolate the analyte from the matrix (**clean-up**),
- **concentrate** it to reach the detection limit,
- convert it into a solvent compatible with the instrument.

The two main techniques in the syllabus are **liquid–liquid extraction (LLE)** and **solid-phase extraction (SPE)**. Protein precipitation (adding acetonitrile, methanol or an acid to plasma and centrifuging) is the quickest but dirtiest option.

## 4.10 Liquid–liquid extraction (LLE)

**General principle.** A solute distributes itself between two immiscible liquids (usually water and an organic solvent) according to the **Nernst distribution law**:

**K (partition coefficient) = C(organic) / C(aqueous)**, constant at a given temperature, for the same molecular species in both phases.

When the solute ionises, only the un-ionised form usually passes into the organic layer. The **distribution ratio D** includes all forms. For a weak acid:

**D = K / (1 + 10^(pH − pKa))**

So acids are extracted from **acidified** solutions and bases from **alkaline** solutions. For a weak acid of pKa 4.5, the un-ionised fraction is 99% at pH 2.5, 50% at pH 4.5 and only 0.1% at pH 7.5.

**Efficiency of repeated extraction.** The fraction left in the aqueous phase after n extractions, each with volume V(org), is:

**q(n) = [V(aq) / (D·V(org) + V(aq))]ⁿ**

**Worked example.** D = 4, aqueous volume 50 ml, 30 ml of solvent available.
- One extraction with 30 ml: q = 50/(4 × 30 + 50) = 0.294, so **70.6%** extracted.
- Three extractions with 10 ml each: q = [50/(4 × 10 + 50)]³ = 0.171, so **82.9%** extracted.
**Several small extractions beat one large one with the same total solvent.**

**Choice of solvent:** immiscible with water; good solubility for the analyte and poor for interferences; suitable density (chloroform and dichloromethane are heavier than water and form the lower layer; ether, ethyl acetate and hexane the upper layer); low boiling point for easy evaporation; low toxicity and flammability; pure, free of peroxides (ether).

**Procedure (separating funnel)**

```text
   sample (aqueous) + buffer to adjust pH
            │
   add organic solvent ──> stopper, invert, shake, vent often ──> stand to separate
            │                                                         │
   drain lower layer / collect upper layer      repeat 2–3 times with fresh solvent
            │
   combine organic extracts ──> dry (anhydrous Na2SO4) ──> evaporate ──> reconstitute ──> analyse
```

1. Adjust pH so the analyte is un-ionised; add salt (**salting out**, for example NaCl) to push polar analytes into the organic layer.
2. Add the solvent, shake gently but thoroughly, releasing pressure through the stopcock.
3. Let the layers separate; run off the lower layer.
4. Repeat with fresh solvent; combine the extracts.
5. **Back-extraction** for clean-up: shake the organic extract with acid (for a base) so the analyte goes back into water as a salt, leaving neutral impurities behind; then basify and re-extract.
6. Dry, evaporate under nitrogen and redissolve in mobile phase.

**Problems and remedies:** **emulsions** (from proteins and surfactants) are broken by centrifugation, adding salt, filtering through glass wool, or gentle swirling instead of vigorous shaking.

**Variants:** continuous extraction for solutes with low D; Soxhlet extraction for solids; ion-pair extraction (adding a counter-ion to extract ionised drugs); supported liquid extraction (the aqueous sample is spread on an inert support and the solvent flows through, avoiding emulsions); liquid–liquid microextraction using microlitre volumes of solvent.

**Advantages:** simple, cheap equipment, wide choice of solvents, good clean-up for many drugs. **Disadvantages:** large solvent volumes, emulsions, time-consuming, hard to automate, uses toxic solvents, sometimes poor recovery of polar compounds.

## 4.11 Solid-phase extraction (SPE)

**General principle.** SPE is a small-scale form of column chromatography. The liquid sample is passed through a cartridge packed with a solid sorbent; the analyte is **retained** on the sorbent while much of the matrix passes through, interferences are **washed** off, and the analyte is then **eluted** with a small volume of a strong solvent. Retention uses the same interactions as chromatography: hydrophobic, polar, or ionic.

```text
   ┌──────┐   1. Condition   2. Equilibrate   3. Load sample   4. Wash        5. Elute
   │ frit │   methanol       water/buffer      analyte (●)      weak solvent   strong solvent
   │▒▒▒▒▒▒│ ← sorbent bed    wets sorbent      retained;        removes        collects ● in
   │▒▒▒▒▒▒│   (C18, silica,                    matrix (○) passes interferences small volume
   │ frit │    ion exchange)
   └──┬───┘ → to waste / collection (vacuum manifold or positive pressure)
```

**The five steps**

1. **Conditioning:** solvate the sorbent (for reversed phase, methanol opens the alkyl chains).
2. **Equilibration:** water or buffer at the sample's pH replaces the methanol; do not let the bed dry.
3. **Sample loading:** apply the pre-treated sample slowly (diluted, pH-adjusted, centrifuged plasma); the analyte is retained.
4. **Washing:** a weak solvent (water or 5% methanol) removes salts, proteins and weakly held interferences.
5. **Elution:** a small volume of strong solvent (methanol, acetonitrile; for ion exchange, a solvent that neutralises the charge) releases the analyte. The eluate is evaporated and reconstituted, or injected directly.

**Sorbents**

| Type | Examples | Retains | Typical elution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reversed phase | C18, C8, phenyl, polymeric (hydrophilic–lipophilic balanced) | Non-polar and moderately polar drugs from aqueous samples | Methanol, acetonitrile |
| Normal phase | Silica, alumina, Florisil, diol, cyano, amino | Polar compounds from non-polar solvents | More polar solvent |
| Ion exchange | Strong cation exchange (SCX, sulfonic acid), strong anion exchange (SAX, quaternary amine), weak exchangers | Charged acids or bases | Change pH or ionic strength |
| Mixed mode | Reversed phase + ion exchange in one bed | Basic or acidic drugs with very clean extracts | Organic solvent with acid or base |

**Formats:** syringe-barrel cartridges (for example 1–6 ml), disks, 96-well plates for automation, pipette tips, and **solid-phase microextraction (SPME)**, in which a coated fibre absorbs analytes from a liquid or headspace and is desorbed directly in a GC injector.

**Important terms:** **capacity** (how much the bed can hold), **breakthrough volume** (sample volume at which analyte starts to pass through unretained), **recovery** (% of analyte collected) and **concentration factor** (sample volume ÷ eluate volume).

**Applications of SPE**

1. Bioanalysis of drugs and metabolites from plasma and urine before HPLC or LC-MS/MS.
2. Concentration of trace pollutants and pesticides from water.
3. Clean-up of herbal and food extracts.
4. Removal of salts and proteins (desalting peptides).
5. Fractionation of complex mixtures by class.

## 4.12 LLE vs SPE

| Point | Liquid–liquid extraction | Solid-phase extraction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principle | Partition between two immiscible liquids | Adsorption/partition on a solid sorbent |
| Solvent use | Large volumes | Small volumes |
| Emulsions | Common problem | Do not occur |
| Selectivity | Controlled by solvent and pH | Wide range of sorbent chemistries; very selective |
| Concentration of analyte | Limited | High concentration factors |
| Automation | Difficult | Easy (96-well, robots, online SPE) |
| Time | Longer | Shorter, many samples in parallel |
| Cost | Cheap materials | Cartridges add cost |
| Reproducibility | Operator-dependent | Better |

## Remember

- RIA (Yalow and Berson): labelled and unlabelled antigen compete for a limited antibody; bound radioactivity falls as sample antigen rises.
- Components: antigen, tracer (¹²⁵I gamma about 60 days; ³H beta), limited antibody, standards, separation system, counter.
- B/B0 vs log concentration is sigmoid; logit–log is linear; read unknowns in the middle region.
- Separation: charcoal, PEG/ammonium sulfate, double antibody, solid phase. IRMA = labelled antibody in excess, non-competitive.
- Limitations: radiation, waste, short tracer life, cross-reactivity.
- LLE: K = Corg/Caq; acids from acid, bases from base; q(n) = [Vaq/(D·Vorg + Vaq)]ⁿ; several small extractions are better.
- SPE steps: condition → equilibrate → load → wash → elute; sorbents reversed phase, normal phase, ion exchange, mixed mode.

# Unit 5: Hyphenated techniques

A chromatograph separates a mixture but identifies each peak only by its retention time, which many compounds can share. A mass spectrometer identifies a compound by its mass and fragments but struggles with mixtures. Joining the two online gives a technique that separates **and** identifies in one run. Such combinations are called **hyphenated techniques**, because their names are written with a hyphen: GC-MS, LC-MS, HPTLC-MS. With a second stage of mass analysis (MS/MS) they become the most sensitive and selective tools in modern drug analysis.

## 5.1 The idea of hyphenation

**Hyphenated technique:** an online coupling of a separation technique with one (or more) spectroscopic detection techniques, so that each separated component is identified as it emerges.

| Separation | Spectroscopic detector | Hyphenated technique |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas chromatography | Mass spectrometry | GC-MS, GC-MS/MS |
| Liquid chromatography (HPLC, UHPLC) | Mass spectrometry | LC-MS, LC-MS/MS |
| HPTLC | Mass spectrometry | HPTLC-MS |
| Gas chromatography | Infrared | GC-IR (GC-FTIR) |
| Liquid chromatography | NMR | LC-NMR |
| Capillary electrophoresis | Mass spectrometry | CE-MS |
| Inductively coupled plasma | Mass spectrometry | ICP-MS (elements) |

**Advantages of hyphenation**

1. Separation and identification in one run; no need to collect fractions.
2. Very high **selectivity**: two independent properties (retention and mass) must both match.
3. Very high **sensitivity** (pg or even fg amounts with MS/MS).
4. Structural information on unknown peaks (molecular mass, fragments).
5. Peaks that co-elute can still be measured separately if their masses differ.
6. Faster method development and fewer sample handling errors; easy automation.

**The main technical problem is the interface:** the chromatograph works at or above atmospheric pressure with a gas or liquid stream, while the mass analyser needs high vacuum. Every hyphenated technique is defined by how it solves this.

## 5.2 Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS)

**MS/MS** uses two stages of mass analysis with a fragmentation step between them.

```text
  ion source ──> Q1 ──────────> q2 (collision cell) ──────────> Q3 ──────────> detector
               select one       ions collide with argon or      separate or
               precursor ion    nitrogen and break up (CID)      select product ions
               (parent)         into product (daughter) ions
                                         Triple quadrupole (QqQ)
```

- **Q1** acts as a filter and lets through one chosen **precursor ion** (for example [M + H]⁺).
- **q2** is a collision cell (an RF-only quadrupole or hexapole) filled with an inert gas. The precursor ions collide with gas atoms, gain internal energy and break into **product ions**. This is **collision-induced dissociation (CID)**, also called collision-activated dissociation.
- **Q3** analyses the product ions.

**Scan modes**

| Mode | Q1 | Q3 | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Product ion scan** | Fixed on one precursor | Scans | Fragmentation pattern of one compound; structure work |
| **Precursor ion scan** | Scans | Fixed on one product ion | Finds all compounds giving a common fragment (for example a family of metabolites) |
| **Neutral loss scan** | Scans | Scans with a fixed mass offset | Finds all compounds losing the same neutral (for example 80 for sulfate, 176 for glucuronide conjugates) |
| **Selected (multiple) reaction monitoring, SRM / MRM** | Fixed on precursor | Fixed on product | **Quantitation**: very selective and sensitive; several transitions monitored in one run |

**Worked example: paracetamol by MRM.** Paracetamol (C8H9NO2, monoisotopic mass 151.063) gives [M + H]⁺ at m/z **152.1** in positive electrospray. In the collision cell it loses ketene (CH2=C=O, 42.0) from the acetamide group, giving a product ion at m/z **110.1** (152.07 − 42.01 = 110.06). The transition **152 → 110** is monitored. Only a molecule that has mass 152 **and** gives a 110 fragment **and** elutes at paracetamol's retention time is counted, so the plasma background almost disappears.

Other tandem instruments: **Q-TOF** (quadrupole + time of flight, accurate-mass product ions for metabolite identification), **ion trap** (traps ions and fragments them repeatedly, MSⁿ) and Orbitrap-based hybrids.

## 5.3 GC-MS and GC-MS/MS

**Principle.** Volatile, thermally stable compounds are separated on a GC column; each one passes through an interface into the ion source of a mass spectrometer, where it is ionised (usually by EI at 70 eV), and its mass spectrum is recorded every fraction of a second.

**Instrumentation**

```text
 carrier gas (He) ──> injector ──> capillary column in oven ──> heated transfer line ──> EI/CI ion source
                                                                                              │
              data system <── detector (electron multiplier) <── mass analyser (quadrupole, ion trap, TOF)
                                                                  (high vacuum: turbomolecular pump)
```

| Part | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Carrier gas** | Helium (inert, light, does not interfere); hydrogen also used |
| **Injector and column** | Split/splitless injector; fused-silica capillary columns (for example 30 m × 0.25 mm) with low-bleed stationary phases, since column bleed raises MS background |
| **Interface** | With capillary columns (about 1 ml/min of gas) the column end goes **directly into the ion source** through a heated transfer line; the vacuum pumps can remove this small flow. With older packed columns (20–30 ml/min) a **separator** was needed to remove most of the carrier gas: the **jet separator** (light helium atoms spread out of the supersonic jet and are pumped away, while heavier analyte molecules travel straight into the next nozzle), the **effusion (Watson–Biemann) separator** (porous glass through which light helium escapes) and the **membrane separator** (a silicone membrane through which organic molecules dissolve, but helium does not) |
| **Ion source** | EI (library-searchable spectra); CI for molecular mass |
| **Analyser** | Single quadrupole most common; ion trap; TOF; **triple quadrupole for GC-MS/MS** |
| **Data system** | Spectra stored for every scan; library search against reference spectra |

**Data obtained**

- **Total ion chromatogram (TIC):** sum of all ion intensities in each scan plotted against time; looks like a normal chromatogram.
- **Mass spectrum of each peak:** taken from the scans across that peak; identified by library matching.
- **Extracted ion chromatogram (EIC):** intensity of one chosen m/z plotted against time; picks out a compound from co-eluting peaks.
- **Selected ion monitoring (SIM):** the analyser monitors only a few chosen ions instead of scanning; much higher sensitivity for quantitation.
- **MRM (GC-MS/MS):** precursor → product transitions; best selectivity in dirty samples.

**Derivatisation** makes polar, non-volatile drugs suitable for GC-MS: silylation (trimethylsilyl derivatives of OH, COOH, NH), acylation and methylation (esters of acids).

**Advantages:** high resolving power of capillary GC, reproducible EI spectra and large libraries, robust, relatively cheap. **Limitations:** only volatile and thermally stable compounds (or derivatives); large, polar, ionic molecules (peptides, salts) cannot be handled; derivatisation adds steps.

**Applications of GC-MS and GC-MS/MS**

1. **Residual solvents** in drugs (with headspace sampling).
2. **Forensic toxicology and drugs of abuse** in urine and blood; confirmation of screening tests.
3. **Doping control:** anabolic steroids and stimulants in athletes.
4. **Pesticide residues** in herbal drugs, food and water (MS/MS for very low limits).
5. **Essential oils and volatile constituents** of medicinal plants; fingerprinting.
6. **Impurity profiling** of volatile impurities, including potential genotoxic impurities such as alkyl halides.
7. **Environmental analysis:** dioxins, polyaromatic hydrocarbons.
8. **Metabolomics** of small volatile or derivatised metabolites.

## 5.4 LC-MS and LC-MS/MS

**Principle.** Compounds separated by HPLC (or UHPLC) are converted into gas-phase ions **at atmospheric pressure** in an interface (ion source) and then pass into the mass analyser through a small orifice and stages of pumping.

**Why LC-MS is harder than GC-MS.** An HPLC pumps about 0.2–1 ml/min of liquid. Each millilitre of water expands to more than a litre of vapour, far more than a mass spectrometer's vacuum pumps can remove. Early interfaces (moving belt, thermospray, particle beam) were complicated and unreliable. **Atmospheric pressure ionisation (API)** solved the problem by making ions outside the vacuum and letting only the ions (with little solvent) enter.

### Electrospray ionisation (ESI)

```text
 LC eluent ──> metal capillary at high voltage (2–5 kV) ──> Taylor cone ──> spray of charged droplets
                    (nebulising N2 gas around it)                                   │
          heated drying gas evaporates solvent; droplet shrinks; charge density rises│
          droplets split (Coulomb fission at the Rayleigh limit) ─> gas-phase ions ──> sampling cone ──> MS
```

1. The eluent passes through a narrow capillary held at a high voltage; a fine mist of **charged droplets** forms (helped by nebulising nitrogen).
2. Heated drying gas evaporates the solvent. The droplet shrinks while its charge stays the same.
3. When charge repulsion exceeds surface tension (Rayleigh limit) the droplet bursts into smaller droplets (Coulomb fission).
4. Finally ions are released into the gas phase (ion evaporation, or charged residue for large molecules).
5. Ions are drawn through a sampling cone or heated capillary into the vacuum region.

**Features of ESI**
- Very soft: gives [M + H]⁺ or [M + Na]⁺ in positive mode and [M − H]⁻ in negative mode, with little fragmentation.
- Best for **polar and ionic** compounds already charged in solution: most drugs, metabolites, peptides, proteins, nucleotides.
- Large molecules carry **many charges**, so a protein of 15,000 Da appears at m/z values within a normal analyser's range: with 10 protons, m/z = (15,000 + 10 × 1.007)/10 ≈ **1501.0**; with 15 protons, ≈ 1001.0. Two adjacent peaks of the charge envelope give both the charge and the mass. For peaks at m/z 1501.0 and 1364.6, the charge of the 1501.0 peak is (1364.6 − 1.007)/(1501.0 − 1364.6) = 10, and M = 10 × (1501.0 − 1.007) ≈ 15,000.
- Sensitive to **ion suppression** by salts and co-eluting matrix.

### Atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI)

- The eluent is sprayed into a **heated nebuliser** (about 350–500 °C) where solvent and analyte are vaporised.
- A **corona discharge needle** ionises solvent molecules, which then transfer protons to the analyte in the gas phase (as in CI).
- Gives mainly singly charged [M + H]⁺; tolerates higher flow rates.
- Suits **less polar, smaller, thermally stable** compounds that ESI ionises poorly (steroids, some lipophilic drugs).

**Atmospheric pressure photoionisation (APPI)** uses a UV lamp to ionise non-polar compounds; useful where both ESI and APCI fail.

| Point | ESI | APCI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where ions form | In solution, then released from droplets | In the gas phase after vaporisation |
| Energy source | High voltage on capillary | Heat + corona discharge |
| Best analytes | Polar, ionic, large (proteins, peptides) | Medium to low polarity, smaller, thermally stable |
| Multiple charging | Yes | No (singly charged) |
| Flow rate | Low to moderate | Higher flows tolerated |
| Matrix suppression | More | Less |

**Instrumentation of LC-MS/MS**

```text
 mobile phase ─> pump ─> autosampler ─> column (C18) ─> [UV detector optional] ─> API source (ESI/APCI)
                                                                                         │
       data system <── electron multiplier <── Q3 <── q2 collision cell <── Q1 <── ion optics (vacuum stages)
```

**Practical rules for LC-MS mobile phases**

1. Use **volatile** buffers and additives: formic acid, acetic acid, ammonium formate, ammonium acetate, ammonia.
2. Avoid **non-volatile** salts (phosphate, sulfate buffers) and non-volatile ion-pair reagents: they crystallise in the source and suppress ionisation.
3. Use low flow rates or split the flow; narrow-bore and UHPLC columns suit MS.
4. Use a **stable-isotope-labelled internal standard** (for example a deuterated drug) to correct for ion suppression and extraction losses.
5. Clean samples (SPE, protein precipitation; Unit 4) reduce **matrix effects**.

**Advantages of LC-MS/MS:** handles polar, non-volatile and thermally unstable compounds without derivatisation; very low LOQ (pg/ml); high throughput (run times of a few minutes); identification and quantitation together. **Limitations:** expensive; matrix effects; fewer spectral libraries than EI; needs skilled operators.

**Applications of LC-MS and LC-MS/MS**

1. **Bioanalysis for pharmacokinetic, bioavailability and bioequivalence studies:** drug levels in plasma by MRM.
2. **Drug metabolism:** finding and identifying metabolites (precursor ion and neutral loss scans, accurate mass Q-TOF).
3. **Impurity and degradation product identification** in APIs and formulations; trace genotoxic impurities.
4. **Proteins and biopharmaceuticals:** intact mass, peptide mapping, glycosylation (proteomics).
5. **Therapeutic drug monitoring** of immunosuppressants and other narrow-range drugs.
6. **Newborn screening** and clinical biomarkers.
7. **Natural product dereplication:** quickly recognising known compounds in plant extracts.
8. **Doping, forensic and food safety** (antibiotic residues, mycotoxins).

## 5.5 HPTLC-MS

**HPTLC refresher.** High-performance thin layer chromatography uses plates with fine, uniform particles (about 5–6 µm), automated sample application as narrow bands, controlled development chambers and **densitometric scanning** for quantitation. Many samples and standards run side by side on one plate.

**Why couple HPTLC with MS?** A spot or band on a TLC plate is identified only by its Rf and colour reaction. MS gives the molecular mass and fragments of the compound in the zone, confirming its identity without isolating it.

**Ways of coupling**

| Approach | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **Offline scraping** | Scrape the zone, extract with solvent, filter and infuse into MS (simple, slow) |
| **Elution-head interface (TLC-MS interface)** | A plunger with an oval or round head presses on the chosen zone and seals it; solvent from an HPLC pump flows through the layer under the head, dissolves the compound and carries it directly to the ESI or APCI source. Takes about a minute per zone |
| **Direct desorption methods** | **DESI** (desorption electrospray: a charged solvent spray hits the plate surface and releases ions), **DART** (direct analysis in real time: excited gas desorbs and ionises), **MALDI** from the plate after matrix application, laser desorption |

**Steps of HPTLC-MS (elution-head method)**

1. Develop the plate; mark zones under UV light or by densitometry (avoid derivatising reagents on zones meant for MS, or use a parallel track).
2. Position the elution head on the zone using the laser crosshair.
3. Pump a suitable volatile solvent (for example methanol with formic acid or ammonium formate) through the zone.
4. Send the eluate to the MS (optionally through a short column to remove silica fines).
5. Record the spectrum; compare with the reference standard spotted on the same plate.
6. Elute a blank area of the plate as a background check.

**Advantages:** fast identification of selected zones; many samples screened on one plate, only interesting zones sent to MS; low solvent use; ideal for complex herbal extracts. **Limitations:** not continuous (zone by zone); possible interference from binders and plate impurities; lower sensitivity than LC-MS/MS; needs volatile elution solvents.

**Applications of HPTLC-MS**

1. Identification of marker compounds and **fingerprinting of herbal drugs** and botanicals.
2. Detecting **adulterants**, for example synthetic drugs illegally added to herbal or "natural" products.
3. Identifying **unknown impurities and degradation products** found during HPTLC stability studies.
4. Detecting **counterfeit** medicines.
5. Screening food contaminants, dyes and residues.
6. Effect-directed analysis: combining a bioassay on the plate with MS to identify the active zone.

## 5.6 Comparison of the three couplings

| Point | GC-MS/MS | LC-MS/MS | HPTLC-MS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Separation | Gas, capillary column | Liquid, packed column | Planar, silica plate |
| Analytes | Volatile, thermally stable (or derivatised) | Polar, non-volatile, thermally labile, large | Wide range; mainly screening and identification |
| Usual ionisation | EI, CI | ESI, APCI, APPI | ESI/APCI via elution head; DESI, DART, MALDI |
| Interface problem | Small gas flow, direct into source (capillary) | Large solvent load, solved by API | Getting the compound off the plate |
| Library search | Large EI libraries | Limited | Limited |
| Quantitation | Excellent (SIM, MRM) | Excellent (MRM) | Mainly qualitative; quantitation by densitometry |
| Typical pharmacy use | Residual solvents, steroids, forensic work, pesticides | Bioanalysis, metabolites, impurities, biologics | Herbal fingerprinting, adulterant detection |

## Remember

- Hyphenation = online separation + spectroscopic identification; the interface is the key problem.
- MS/MS: Q1 selects precursor → q2 collision cell (CID with Ar or N2) → Q3 analyses products. Product, precursor, neutral loss scans; MRM for quantitation.
- Paracetamol MRM 152 → 110 (loss of ketene, 42).
- GC-MS: helium, capillary column straight into EI source; jet, effusion and membrane separators for packed columns; TIC, EIC, SIM; derivatise polar drugs.
- LC-MS: API sources. ESI (charged droplets, multiply charged proteins, polar analytes); APCI (heated vaporiser + corona needle, less polar); APPI (UV lamp).
- Use volatile buffers; avoid phosphate; isotope-labelled internal standard against ion suppression.
- HPTLC-MS: elution-head interface or DESI/DART/MALDI; herbal fingerprinting and adulterant detection.
